# Checkwright installer — design record

The mechanism behind the activation path: what the bootstraps hand to, what each verb does and refuses, what an install records, how the package is assembled, and what asserts all of it end to end. `installer/README.md` is the usage tier in front of this file — what an adopter runs; this file is why it is built that way.

This file is not named on `installer/package.json`'s `files` roster, so it ships in neither the npm tarball nor the Release tarball. [§Layout](#layout) rules that the roster and not the directory listing decides what is reachable at an installed `PKG_ROOT`, which is the same rule the payload applies to a kit's `SPEC.md`, reaching the package one layer out.

## The dependency boundary

This package is not a dependency channel. Nothing resolves at your build time, and nothing is fetched after this package itself. The installer writes no dependency reference, no lockfile entry pointing at a registry, and no install-time lifecycle script. Remove the installer afterwards and the tree it vendored keeps working, needing nothing from a package registry again. That is what one-shot vendoring means, and it is why the vendored-committed doctrine survives the installer. Both properties are asserted, not claimed: [§The consumer smoke](#the-consumer-smoke) installs from a packed tarball with no registry access and runs the whole path from it, and `check-installer-no-deps` reds the package the moment it declares a dependency field or an install-time script.

**The two registries stand in different relations to that.** crates.io holds the name only (`reserve/`): there is nothing to `cargo add`. npm carries a real package, and it is an installer, not a dependency. The same payload also downloads from every tagged GitHub Release, as a tarball and its `.sha256`. A tarball downloaded, verified against its published digest and extracted before anything runs is the most auditable form of the same vendoring. These are two transports over one install model, not two products: both reach the same `init`, write the same `checkwright.lock` and leave the same vendored tree. Only the fetch differs.

**The tarball is the primary path because it removes a runtime dependency.** docs/install.md says so in prose, and its `install-primary:` declaration under §Install is the machine-readable form of the same claim ([canon-kit/SPEC.md §check-install-claim](../canon-kit/SPEC.md#check-install-claim) binds the two). npm stays because it carries a build attestation: `npm publish --provenance` has the release runner sign a statement of what built the package, which a self-hosted asset cannot offer. Neither path dominates, so both properties are named.

**The one-line install.** Each system's section of the install page leads with one line: `curl -fsSL https://checkwright.dev/install.sh | sh`, or `irm https://checkwright.dev/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows. The line fetches a script the docs site serves from this repository, `docs/install.sh` or its PowerShell twin. That script is the recipe below and nothing else. It downloads one pinned release and its digest, verifies it and unpacks it outside the working tree. It then runs the bootstrap from the caller's directory with the caller's arguments (`init` by default), and removes what it unpacked.

- **Arguments and overrides.** Arguments ride `sh -s -- <args>`, or `& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm …))) <args>` on Windows. `CHECKWRIGHT_VERSION` installs a named older release. `CHECKWRIGHT_RELEASE_BASE` replaces the download base; it exists for the CI witness, because `irm` cannot read `file://`.
- **The pin.** The script is tracked text at a named version, so what runs is what this repository reviewed. The pin moves only to a published tag ([§Versioning](#versioning)), so the line never names a release that does not exist yet. The script adds no dependency to the recipe's own.
- **Truncation and status.** Each body is a single function called on the last line, so a truncated fetch runs nothing. The sh script exits with the bootstrap's status. The PowerShell twin never calls `exit`, because text run by `iex` shares the reader's session and `exit` would close it. It leaves the bootstrap's status in `$LASTEXITCODE`, throws naming the step that failed before it, and scopes every preference it sets to its one function. It reads its native steps' status from `$LASTEXITCODE` rather than from a thrown error, because Windows PowerShell wraps a native stderr line in an error record when its output is redirected.
- **The served encoding.** GitHub Pages serves the PowerShell twin as `application/octet-stream`: `.ps1` has no text mapping there, and Pages takes no header config. Windows PowerShell 5.1's `irm` still yields a string for that type, but decodes it in a single-byte charset, so a non-ASCII byte reaches `iex` changed. `check-portability-floor`'s ASCII arm confines the twin's non-ASCII bytes to full-line comments ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §check-portability-floor](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#check-portability-floor)). The PowerShell install-smoke leg reads the live URL under 5.1 on every push, and asserts a string that parses and differs from the served text on comment lines only.
- **The honest limit.** Piping runs the script before the reader reads it, unless they fetch it first. The script is served from the site's own TLS origin, so trusting it means trusting the site: one origin more than the recipe, which trusts only the release host. The recipe stays on the page for the reader who reviews each step first.

**The recipe's shape.** Below the line, each system carries the same install as four steps: download, verify, extract, run. macOS and Linux use `sh`, and Windows uses PowerShell. Each recipe unpacks outside the repository, because `init` refuses a worktree that is not clean, and an extracted `package/` in the root is exactly such untracked content. The version is set once, on the recipe's first line. The `package/` prefix comes from `npm pack`: npm builds the asset on the release runner, and consuming it needs no Node.

The Windows recipe names `tar.exe` under the system directory. The `windows-remedy` block puts Git's `usr\bin` ahead of it on `PATH`, and Git's GNU `tar` reads a drive-letter path as a remote host. The recipe runs the bootstrap under `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass`, scoped to that one process, because Windows' default policy refuses a downloaded script.

**The checksum's honest limit.** The digest travels from the same origin, over the same encrypted session, as the tarball. Verifying it catches a corrupted or truncated download, and is no evidence that the release host was uncompromised. The property that carries that is a build attestation, which the npm channel's `--provenance` mints and this channel does not.

## Implementation

POSIX sh, up to the boundary [§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary) rules, and that boundary is the **bootstrap itself**. The two bootstraps are the whole of the shell: one POSIX sh and one PowerShell, twins rather than an original and a rewrite, because the host the second exists for may run no POSIX shell. Everything they hand to the verified gate binary is Rust, every verb included, so an install is written once in one language.

npm is the delivery vehicle, never the implementation. **Both** `bin` entries are scripts, so a reader reviewing what they are about to run reads source rather than a build product. The repository's script linter governs the POSIX one, in the dialect its `#!/bin/sh` selects. The PowerShell half has no linter here, and its oracle is its own install-smoke leg, the trade [§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary)'s parity ruling accepts. What the two scripts do is fixed by that section's step sequence, which the POSIX half labels step by step in its `# spec:` comments, so a reader has no third thing to review before running an install.

**The POSIX half is run by the host's own `/bin/sh`**, so the unix install floor is git, `/bin/sh` and the base userland the bootstrap reads, with no `bash`. POSIX sh is the subset of bash the OS's `/bin/sh` also runs, the reading of the bash-for-Linux-and-macOS policy the generated hooks rest on ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §gen-pre-commit](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#gen-pre-commit)). Writing to that subset costs four things, each settled here:

- **The payload directory comes from `$0`.** The bootstrap is executed, never sourced, so `$0` is its path, and npm's `bin` link is resolved with plain `readlink`. `CDPATH` is unset before the first `cd`: a POSIX `cd` into a relative path consults it and prints the directory it picked, which would corrupt the `$( )` capturing `pwd`. Whether `readlink`'s answer is already rooted is asked of `gate_path_rooted`, which the bootstrap carries as a byte twin of gate-sdk's library body, held to it by a crate unit test ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §lib/gate.sh](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#libgatesh)).
- **No `local`.** POSIX has none and a `/bin/sh` that is not dash, bash or a BSD sh may lack it, so the functions share the script's scope and every working name is unique within the file.
- **No `pipefail`.** No pipeline's verdict needs it: the roster test reads the last `grep`'s, and step 4 reads what it captured — a hasher that fails leaves the computed digest empty, which the empty-or-unequal test already refuses.
- **Pattern tests are `case`, the rest `[ ]`**, and artifact selection is a glob ([§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary)), so no array, process substitution or `find` primary is used.

macOS's `/bin/sh` is bash in POSIX mode, a lenient runner, so the dialect claim rests on `check-shellcheck` and on the Linux install-smoke legs, whose `/bin/sh` is dash.

## Requirements

This package reaches a tree over two transports, and each carries its own requirement. The install page's prerequisites block lists each transport's tools and their floors, one row per tool, naming the systems that need it. Those tools serve a delivery path alone. The vendored battery uses Node on no path, no delivery-path tool joins the toolchain roster, and the manual vendoring path ([§Vendoring without the installer](#vendoring-without-the-installer)) needs nothing beyond that roster. A consumer who would rather not add Node takes another path and loses nothing. The toolchain the battery does assert, with its version floors, is on the install page; the contributor's is in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

**One requirement belongs to `init` itself, whichever transport delivered it: `sha256sum` or `shasum`.** The bootstrap verifies the gate binary against its published digest before running it, and a host with neither hasher is refused rather than given a smaller install ([§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary)). This is the one step that cannot use the binary to verify the binary; behind the invoke, the binary hashes in-process. The requirement sits beside the roster rather than in it, because the roster lists what the battery requires, and the battery does not require a hasher.

**The install page's requirement blocks, and why each reads as it does.** The page renders seven marker blocks. Its opening [§Requirements](#requirements) holds three tables: platform, toolchain and prerequisites. Each OS section holds that system's remedy block and, inside its collapsed step-by-step form, its install block. Each block is held by a reader, and [docs/site-architecture.md §Generated projections and their freshness gates](https://github.com/checkwright/checkwright/blob/master/docs/site-architecture.md#generated-projections-and-their-freshness-gates) owns those contracts: the platform and toolchain parity, and the legs of the remedy and install blocks. The grounds the page's prose leaves out are these.

- **Platform posture.** Checkwright is Unix-first. The engine assumes the POSIX userland `GATE_SDK_PROGRAM_FLOOR` names ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §lib/gate.sh](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#libgatesh)), and no shipped adopter path needs GNU coreutils. Native Windows is a joined platform: the gate binary is published for it, `install-smoke-pwsh-windows` installs that published build, and Git for Windows supplies the bash and the userland. The requirements state what a native Windows host must satisfy, not a promise about one. WSL is a route an adopter may choose instead, served by the Linux line. The platform block declares the narrower fact of whether an install is possible at all: a platform the roster does not carry is refused, because every step of an install is behind the binary ([§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary)). Each Linux architecture has two artifacts. The glibc one's floor is the glibc symbol set it binds, measured by the shared build body on a pinned image. The static musl one's floor is the kernel, declared from Rust's platform support, and the build body refuses it if it links anything dynamically. A host meets the glibc artifact where it runs and the musl one everywhere else ([§Selection](#selection)).
- **The macOS remedy.** Stock macOS ships bash 3.2, below the 4.3 floor. That floor binds only where the selected profile carries a kit that owes `bash`, so a starter or prose install needs no remedy. The block is the whole remedy. It installs a current bash from Homebrew and puts Homebrew's `bin` ahead of `/bin` on `PATH`, both in `~/.zprofile` (the profile a new zsh Terminal reads) and in the running shell. The requirements check what `PATH` actually resolves, so a Mac whose Homebrew bash is not first on `PATH` reaches the system's 3.2. The two macOS install-smoke legs run the block verbatim, then open a fresh login shell and source the line it appended, so both the ordering and its persistence are measured.
- **The Windows remedy.** Git's installer puts only its `cmd` directory on `PATH` by default, and that directory holds no userland. The block adds Git's `usr\bin` and `bin` for the session and, through the user `Path`, for every later one. `install-smoke-pwsh-windows` runs it verbatim under PowerShell. `uninstall` reverses neither remedy, since it touches the repository and not the machine.
- **The install blocks.** Each OS section's recipe is split at the network. A fetch fence only a published release can serve comes first. A marked install block (verify, extract, run) follows, and the install-smoke legs run it verbatim against a packed tarball placed where the fetch would have put it. Everything after the download is therefore measured on the host it is written for, and only the two download lines are left to the release. The Windows block runs the bootstrap under Windows PowerShell 5.1, the one PowerShell every Windows host carries, and its leg holds the bootstrap to that host. That host is why the bootstrap's code stays ASCII outside its comments. 5.1 reads a BOM-less script in the ANSI code page, where a UTF-8 em-dash decodes to a closing double quote and ends the string around it; a BOM would break the `#!/usr/bin/env pwsh` line npm's shim reads. `check-portability-floor`'s ASCII arm holds it at commit, over every `.ps1` on the configured install-path corpus ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §check-portability-floor](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#check-portability-floor)).
- **The one-line witness.** After the install block, the same two legs run each one-line install as an adopter runs it: `curl … | sh` into the Linux runner's dash, and `irm … | iex` under Windows PowerShell. The tarball and digest the install block placed are served as a release from a local web server, with both overrides set. Each leg asserts the install's status and a written `checkwright.lock`. It then pipes the script into a second consumer in the page's argument form, `sh -s --` or the script block: `init --profile starter`, asserting the recorded profile, then `uninstall`, asserting the lock removed. A dropped argument list runs the default `init`, which leaves the lock, so the `uninstall` pass is what observes one. The local server is the witness's own tool and no adopter's. The witness does not reach the served copy at the live URL, the content type the site sends for `.ps1`, or TLS: its transport is local and unencrypted.
- **The pin rule.** A toolchain member is pinned only where a construct the battery actually runs forces the pin, and each pinned member names that construct. A prerequisite no construct forces says `any` rather than leaving the cell blank, so a reader can tell a considered absence from an omission. A floor nobody's code forces is an aspiration, and an aspiration is what rots.
- **The audience token.** A toolchain row's Needed cell names whose floor it is, and an optional row states the condition that owes it. `contributors` marks a tool nothing on an install path reaches: its row sits in `CONTRIBUTING.md` rather than on the install page, and `doctor` leaves it out of its verdict entirely. `optional: if you register a gate that runs it` holds only where a gate registered in `gates.list` needs the tool. `optional: if your profile includes …` holds only where the profile carries a named kit, several listed where it carries any of them. `required` binds every adopter's machine. `doctor` run outside an install names a selection-bound member as *not probed* rather than guessing a selection. The roster lives in `native/src/toolfloor.rs` beside the floor predicate that reads it, and the two tables render it.
- **The `bash` audience.** The kits owing `bash` are those shipping a file the host runs with bash. The list is derived at probe time by the predicate [context-kit/SPEC.md §bin/env-probe](../context-kit/SPEC.md#binenv-probe) states, so a kit that later ships such a file joins it with nobody remembering to. Prose telling a reader to type a bash command does not meet that predicate. The starter and prose profiles reach none of those kits until a consumer's docs mark a fence runnable: canon-kit's `check-fence-run` then runs it with `bash`, and canon-kit joins the list from the next `doctor`. A shell gate an adopter writes is outside the audience, because it is not a kit file and the derivation cannot see it. The install page states that requirement in prose, native Windows included, where Git for Windows' bash is the only shell a custom gate runs under.
- **What runs without `bash`.** Both generated git hooks are two-line POSIX sh handing off to the gate binary, and the unix install bootstrap (`installer/bin/checkwright.sh`) is POSIX sh. All run under `/bin/sh`, and on native Windows the hooks run under the sh Git for Windows bundles, so installing a starter or prose profile reaches no `bash` either. On native Windows a front-end battery runs from PowerShell through `gate-sdk/bin/run-gates.ps1`. Git for Windows' bundled bash serves guard-kit's hook, because the harness runs both its `Bash` tool and its hook commands under that shell.
- **The `bash` floor.** 4.3 is the highest construct the shipped shell runs: a nameref (`local -n`) in the gate library, which every kit shell surface that reads a knob before locating the binary sources. Associative arrays, `mapfile` and the lowercasing case expansion reach only 4.0. A GNU-only construct the shipped shell uses is named here and cited by a `# portability-declared:` marker at its site. The declaration and the enforcement are so one fact with one owner, and `check-portability-floor` reds a new undeclared use.
- **The self-check is the binary.** The page's machine check is the gate binary's `--emit env-probe` ([context-kit/SPEC.md §bin/env-probe](../context-kit/SPEC.md#binenv-probe)), not a shell front end. The toolchain block states `bash` as owed only by the kits that ship one, and a step that spawned bash would ask every reader for a tool most of them do not need. The check reports each tool's version *and* its verdict against the contract, so the profile answers whether the box qualifies.
- **The docs-site tier.** Publishing a docs site is an optional wider tier. A consumer registering site-kit's render-fidelity gate, which re-renders every page through the GitHub Pages parser, also needs Ruby with the `kramdown-parser-gfm` gem, and the `liquid` gem where it registers the Liquid-parse gate. A consumer publishing no site installs neither. Their versions are the prerequisites block's rows.
- **The prerequisites block.** It carries what the roster does not, because none of it is probed. The install path's tools are needed before a binary exists to probe them, and the docs gates' renderer is a knob-supplied command no `REGISTRY` row names. Arm F of `check-install-platforms` holds that every row states a Minimum and every declared system has a row.

**Neither the verbs nor anything they install need `jq`.** The verbs read JSON (this package's version stamp and the `checkwright.lock` manifest) with the crate's own parser, so none refuses for want of an external one. guard-kit's hook is a member of the gate binary, which reads its payload and renders its envelopes itself ([guard-kit/SPEC.md §The shell guard](../guard-kit/SPEC.md#the-shell-guard)). So `jq` is on the toolchain floor for contributors alone. `doctor` owes it to no selection, and every profile, guard-kit's included, installs on a machine without it. `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s toolchain table names it for the smoke harnesses that still read JSON with it.

## Layout

- `bin/checkwright.sh` — the POSIX sh bootstrap ([§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary)), run by the host's own `/bin/sh`, and the package's `bin` entry. npm's shim generator takes the interpreter from its `#!/bin/sh` line, which the extension-less shim MSYS runs resolves and the `.cmd` shim does not; a native Windows adopter is sent to `checkwright-pwsh` below, so no supported path runs through that `.cmd` shim.
- `bin/checkwright.ps1` — the PowerShell bootstrap ([§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary)), the second `bin` entry, named `checkwright-pwsh` there. npm generates `<name>.cmd` and `<name>.ps1` shims itself, so a second entry also named `checkwright` would collide with the shim npm writes for the sh target. **Its `#!/usr/bin/env pwsh` line is load-bearing**: npm's shim generator reads the target's shebang to pick the interpreter, and without one writes a shim invoking the `.ps1` directly, which a Windows host cannot do.
- `payload/` — the vendored kit source, assembled at pack time from the repository's own kit roots. It exists in the published tarball only, never in the source tree, so no second copy of any kit is checked in. The gate binary sits at `payload/artifact/<target>/`, and a running binary finds its package from that location alone. A copy reached anywhere else, the one `init` places in a consumer's tree above all, resolves no package and meets the no-payload refusal.
- `recipes/` — the payload recipes ([§Payload recipes](#payload-recipes)), assembled at pack time from the directories `GATE_SDK_PAYLOAD_RECIPES` names, never tracked here.
- `profiles.list` — the profile rosters (below).
- `LICENSE` — the license text, placed at pack time from the repository root ([§The packer](#the-packer)), never tracked here.
- `action.yml` — the CI action ([§The CI action](#the-ci-action)). It sits in this directory because the activation surface does, and it is off the `files` roster, so neither package carries it.

**There is no `lib/`.** Every verb lives behind the invoke, in the gate binary the payload carries, so the package ships two bootstraps and a payload and nothing between them.

**`package.json`'s `files` roster, not the directory listing, decides what is reachable at an installed `PKG_ROOT`.** Its entries are **directories**, so `bin/` publishes both bootstraps, and naming either on it would declare twice what the directory entry carries. A directory that stops existing must also leave the roster, a separate edit.

## The verbs

`init` makes an install; the rest manage one after it exists. Each is a `--`-prefixed arm of the gate binary, reached through the bootstrap's one argv rule ([§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary), step 5). **The roster's owner is the binary**: a verb is advertised because the artifact carries it, so `checkwright --help` cannot promise one this build lacks, and the binary's own usage arm refuses an unknown one. The same holds for flags: `FLAGS` beside `VERBS` names each flag and the verbs that accept it, and a crate test holds every parser and `usage:` line to it.

Every verb answers `-h`/`--help` on its own, before any precondition and from any argv position, and refuses an unknown argument at exit 2. A refusal carries the verb's own `checkwright <verb>:` prefix, an optional `help:` line and an exit status. What each verb is *for*:

| verb | asks | reads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `init` | vendor this profile's kits into my repository | the payload, and the manifest a previous run left |
| `doctor` | can this machine run the battery, and what is installed here? | the toolchain, and the manifest's identity fields |
| `diff` | which of the files `init` wrote have I changed? | the manifest's `files` hashes, against the tree |
| `update` | bring the install here up to the version this package carries | the manifest, then everything `init` reads |
| `uninstall` | reverse the install, keeping anything I have edited | the manifest's `files` roster, against the tree |
| `demo` | show me the adoption arc without touching my repository | the payload, in a scratch repository of its own |

**The classifier is writes / does not write, and it decides `--dry-run`.** `doctor` and `diff` write nothing, and `demo` writes only into a scratch repository it makes and removes ([§demo](#demo)), so none of the three takes one. Every verb that writes does, with one meaning: print the plan, write nothing, exit 0. [§The consumer smoke](#the-consumer-smoke) asserts it behaviorally: `init`, `update` and `uninstall --dry-run` each leave the tree object and the worktree unchanged over a consumer the real run would change.

**`diff` is a verb of its own, not a widening of `doctor`**, on two independent grounds:

- `doctor`'s exit status has one owner, the toolchain contract, and `init` gates its precondition on it. [§doctor](#doctor) already reports an artifact finding without setting the status, since reddening would block the `init` re-run that fixes it. Editing a vendored file is **sanctioned** ([§The manifest](#the-manifest)), so a folded-in drift report would be a permanent expected finding. Drift wants a status of its own, `0` the tree is what `init` wrote and `1` it diverged, which CI can gate on and which would collide with the toolchain's number.
- `doctor` runs before every install, so per-file hashing there would make every `init` pay for a computation the install repeats moments later.

The `--dry-run`s do not stand in for it: they answer *what would this payload change*, and an adopter deciding whether to uninstall needs *what have I changed* without running a mutating verb.

## init

`checkwright init` vendors the selected kit set, a profile's adjusted by any selection ([§Selecting kits and gates](#selecting-kits-and-gates)), out of this package's own payload into your repository, and commits it. What governs your tree afterwards is committed and auditable on the terms [gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload) sets.

**No selection builds.** `init` writes files and compiles nothing, so it asks for **no build toolchain** and cannot fail on one. The only toolchain it asks for is the one the vendored battery runs, which the `doctor` precondition checks. A compiled gate arrives as a prebuilt binary picked for your platform and checked against a published digest before it is written ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Porting a gate to the binary substrate](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#porting-a-gate-to-the-binary-substrate), criterion 5).

**Three preconditions, each refusing rather than warning**, and each checked before a single file is written, since a partial install is the outcome none may produce:

- **You are inside a git work tree.** The vendored source is meant to be committed, which is what makes it auditable.
- **The worktree is clean.** `init` makes one commit, and a dirty tree would fold your work into it. A clean start also attributes a run's residue: anything dirty at a recorded path when the run ends was written by that run, which lets a no-op run commit what it rewrote. `--no-commit` is the valve. It stages the files and leaves the commit to you, waiving the precondition and that attribution with it.
- **`doctor` passes.** It holds you to the floor the selected kit set owes, the tools the vendored battery runs, never one that only builds Checkwright ([§doctor](#doctor)). `init` resolves the kit set first and refuses at exit 2 one resolving to no kit or a selection it cannot honour, since the kit set is half of what `doctor` reads. A machine below the floor is refused before any write, never halfway through.

  Every refusal `init` makes about the machine is this one. *This package carries no version stamp* and *`checkwright.lock` carries a schema this build does not know* are about the package and the manifest, reached by the crate's own JSON reader, and each means exactly what it names.

It writes the kit directories, a `gates.list` seeded with each kit's starting gates, the config seams those kits need, and the manifest. It makes **one commit** naming the profile and the version, then prints a **follow-up block**: the commands that finish the setup, each with its reason. Each runs the binary `init` placed by its root-relative path prefixed `./`, with the artifact's executable suffix, a spelling both `sh` and PowerShell run with no interpreter before it. `install-smoke-pwsh-windows` runs the printed lines from PowerShell and commits through the hooks they wire. The commands are not spelled on this page: what `init` prints is `init`'s to say.

**The block has a stated grammar, because [§The consumer smoke](#the-consumer-smoke)'s follow-up arm reads it**, so a reflow reds that arm rather than silently un-covering it:

- the banner line is exactly `next:`;
- each following line that begins with whitespace and then a non-whitespace character is one command, and the block ends at the first other line or at the end of the output;
- on a command line, everything from the first `#` is commentary for the adopter;
- the **target** is the first token containing a `/`, any token before it the interpreter, and every later token beginning with `-` a flag.

**An install's size is not bounded by the host's argv width.** `init` names every vendored path to `git` when it stages and when it asks what the run left behind, and a large roster can overflow the command line a host accepts (`Argument list too long`). Those calls go in batches, so a profile's size is bounded by the payload alone. The binding ceiling is a native Windows process limit that `getconf` does not report, so the batch size is a fixed conservative budget.

**Re-running is idempotent and non-destructive.** A second `init` reads each recorded hash from the manifest. A file still at its hash is `init`'s to rewrite, and one changed since is **yours**, reported and left alone unless you pass `--force`. The protection outlives upgrades and a release that stops shipping the file: the path stays on the roster at `init`'s hash, so a release re-adding it meets the same protection. The gate binary is the one exception ([§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary)). A re-run with nothing to change says so and exits clean.

**"Nothing to change" still commits what the run rewrote.** `init` regenerates its vendored tools' projections on every run, and **one commit** is a promise about what the run leaves behind. So the no-op exit commits anything it rewrote that is uncommitted, under the vendoring commit's message, and says so; under `--no-commit` the arm is off. That commit sits **inside** the exit, never ahead of it, because a commit against an empty index fails and `init` treats a failed commit as fatal.

**The commit passes the hooks it vendors.** A re-run on a clone with hooks installed commits through them, and an `update` or profile move stages the manifest beside the gate files it rewrites. `check-gate-tamper` counts the manifest as meta-layer ([delegation-kit/SPEC.md §Verify after every agent commit](../delegation-kit/SPEC.md#verify-after-every-agent-commit)), so that commit is isolated rather than refused. The consumer smoke's hooked move arm is the witness.

**A failed commit relays git's own account.** The files stay staged and `init` exits 1, first printing what git and any hook it ran wrote. Its own refusal line cannot say whether a hook's red or a missing git identity stopped the commit, and the remedy differs.

**Each projection lands where your knobs put it.** The hooks go to `GATE_SDK_HOOKS_DIR` and the coupling graph to `GATE_SDK_GRAPH_ARTIFACT`, resolved from your gates directory's knob files as a battery run at the root resolves them. A re-run so writes, records and stages the file your `check-graph` reads. A knob pointing outside the repository gets its file written but not recorded, since `files` holds repo-relative paths ([§The manifest](#the-manifest)). `init` compares no freshness, and the projections stay `init`'s `files` entries.

**A payload older than the recorded install is refused as a silent downgrade.** "Older" is the floor predicate's comparison ([context-kit/SPEC.md §bin/env-probe](../context-kit/SPEC.md#binenv-probe)), over dotted digit runs only, so a prerelease or build suffix is unordered and never reads as a downgrade ([§Versioning](#versioning)). `--force` means one thing in all three places it appears, the changed-file protection, the downgrade refusal and `uninstall`'s kept files ([§uninstall](#uninstall)): overwrite what `init` would otherwise protect.

`--dry-run` prints the file plan and the manifest that would be written, writes nothing, and exits 0. It is **end to end**: a step behind the binary invoke is passed `--dry-run` and honors it ([§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary)), so the plan is the real run's own code, and each seed arm reads one absence test in both modes. The hooks cannot be generated before the binary is placed, so the plan asks the generator's own conditional, whether a registered member is `tier=commit-msg`, of the registry and kit sources the run leaves. *The honest bound:* a kept gate file whose manifest names another tier is read at the payload's tier.

## What init seeds

Beyond the kit directories, `init` writes the least that makes the battery green on the tree it just made.

The **config seam is derived, never listed**: a kit's consumer config is whatever `templates/*-config.sh` or `templates/*-config.knobs` it ships, seeded into your gates directory under the file's own name, so a kit growing a template needs no edit here. Template and seeded copy are **the edit seam, whatever its substrate** ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §The config-seam port disposition](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#the-config-seam-port-disposition)): these are the files you edit, and a port would leave nothing to edit. A kit with static knobs ships a comment-only knob file ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §The knob file](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#the-knob-file)), valid in the grammar as seeded. `init` never deletes a file a release stopped shipping ([§init](#init)), so a shell config an earlier release seeded stays at upgrade, and the reader's legacy refusal names the migration.

**The vendored tree's kit-root set is declared, not inferred.** On every install the placement op, the seam's one writer ([§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary)), writes `GATE_SDK_KIT_DIRS` into `<gates-dir>/gate-sdk-config.knobs` with the selected kit set, exactly what was copied in and what `kits` records. gate-sdk's derived resolver admits a root by `checks/` or `smoke/` on disk, and the payload withholds `smoke/` ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload)). So a kit shipping no `checks/` would drop out **silently**, and a battery over a smaller set is still green. `GATE_SDK_KIT_DIRS` is the override gate-sdk already carries, so the declaration mints no name. [§The consumer smoke](#the-consumer-smoke) counts the resolved roots rather than reading a verdict, since green cannot witness a set that quietly shrank.

**Everything `init` seeds takes one of two disciplines**, by whether `init` keeps rewriting the file:

- **Create-once surfaces**, the queue file, the agent file, the evidence manifests, the workflow-state file and the CI workflow, are written **only when absent**, so a re-run never disturbs a tree that has grown since. The write is recorded unclaimed: a seed you deleted is re-seeded and recorded at its new hash, never reported as your change.
- **Every-run surfaces**, each kit's config seam and gate-sdk's `msg-patterns.list`, are **claimed before they are written**, on the non-destructive path of any vendored file. The recipe *plans* the copy and `init` performs it, so your edit is compared against the recorded hash while it is still on disk; landing the copy first would destroy that evidence.

**`init` also makes the scratch directory, which is not a seed.** gate-sdk's helper creates `GATE_SDK_TMP_DIR` with its self-ignoring `.gitignore` ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Layout and configuration](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#layout-and-configuration)). git never sees the file, so it enters no commit or manifest record and `uninstall` leaves the directory alone. It is made at install so a writer running before the first battery, a harness hook among them, finds it already ignored.

**The queue file's source is resolved once per install, over the whole kit set.** A kit declares itself the queue format's owner by shipping `templates/TASK-QUEUE.md`, and `init` seeds from the first kit in the selected set that ships one. So a kit that reads the queue and ships no template cannot pre-empt one that does. Only when **no** kit ships one is a minimal inline skeleton written, carrying every `QUEUE_KIT_REQUIRED_SECTIONS` heading at that knob's default. A shipping profile takes that path: `prose` reads the queue and ships no template, and the section gate is `on-surface`, so nothing `init` registers would catch a missing heading.

**The CI workflow is seeded when the package names a GitHub repository.** `init` writes `.github/workflows/gates.yml` only when it is absent. It holds one job on `ubuntu-latest`:

- it triggers on a push to the branch `init` ran on (any branch from a detached `HEAD`) and on every pull request, and checks the tree out with its full history;
- it runs the CI action ([§The CI action](#the-ci-action)), naming `package.json`'s `repository` and the payload's `commit` as a full SHA with the version as a trailing comment, the form [gate-sdk/SPEC.md §check-action-pinning](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#check-action-pinning) holds, and pins the checkout step the same way;
- it declares `contents: read` and `security-events: write`, and carries no `run:` body.

A package whose `repository` is not a GitHub URL, or whose `commit` is unstamped, seeds nothing and says so. The body is rendered from a template in `native/src/installer/`, the slug derived from `repository.url` and the checkout pin a recipe constant. The file is recorded in `files`, so `diff`, `uninstall` and the `--dry-run` plan reach it by their existing rules. **Honest limits:** the ref stays at the release that seeded it, while the binary it runs follows the lock. A tree hosted elsewhere carries a file nothing runs, and deleting it does not stick, since a deleted create-once seed is re-seeded.

The **starting gate roster** is the subset a fresh consumer begins with, not the kit's full roster, the distinction gate-sdk's own README draws. A gate whose subject you have not authored has nothing to read, as canon-kit's duplication gate lacks a glossary and site-kit's a docs host, so it is registered when the surface exists. Each kit's README names the full roster to grow into. **No lifecycle-kit gate is `zero-config`**, for per-gate reasons. Some read a stage attestation only a stage session writes, others read surfaces a stage session authors, and `check-lifecycle-registration` and `check-merge-attrs` read what the adopter's own `--install-lifecycle` arm writes.

**A kit's agent-file block is seeded at install iff a gate registered at install reads it.** doctrine-kit's is seeded because `check-doctrine-registration` declares `zero-config`, so the block is read on day one. lifecycle-kit's is not: nothing `init` registers reads it, and seeding it would charge every session's context for machinery nothing yet enforces. The agent-file *membership* predicate asks a different question, whether the file must *exist* for a kit's starting gates, which context-kit answers yes to while writing nothing into it.

**The roster is derived from the gates themselves.** The recipe's per-kit derivation is the **whole** of a fresh consumer's registry, never inferred from a kit's full roster or this repo's `gates.list`. It reads each shipped gate's `# install: <disposition>` line and takes every `zero-config` member ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §The install disposition](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#the-install-disposition)). It carries no gate name, which `check-install-disposition`'s third assertion holds, so a new zero-config gate needs no edit there. One function unions the result over a kit set, and its one caller is the registry `init` writes, which the recipe drops and the selection then adjust. The consumer smoke's monotonicity assertion reads **that registry** across the package boundary, holding no second copy of the derivation, so containment is asserted over what each profile's adopter receives. The roster takes the profile as well as the kit, though no disposition varies on it today, so a roster that does vary is a change to one gate and not to every caller.

**What the seam can and cannot express.** `full` is the payload-derived maximum, so monotonicity means *anything a profile registers, `full` must register too*: a gate armed "for one profile only" is simply `zero-config`. `starter` sits below every profile, so no profile may **drop** a gate-sdk `zero-config` member either. Subtraction between them has nothing to derive from, since the recipe may name no gate and no gate declares profile-varying reachability. So the parameter is **additively inert** and subtractively undeclarable, and a cohort a narrow profile should receive arrives as a disposition correction on each gate.

**A disposition change reaches trees already installed.** `init` rewrites `gates.list` from this derivation, so a gate moving `on-surface` → `zero-config` joins an existing consumer's battery on its next run. Their edits to the file stay protected, since `gates.list` is claimed before it is written, and a release carrying such a move owes them the sentence in its note.

Each kit's `smoke/install.sh` registers a **richer** roster against the tree it builds, a superset of this one by contract, held by `check-install-disposition`. The disposition is what a kit owns; the roster is what each caller derives.

## Payload recipes

A **payload recipe** fits the kits to a tree some other tool lays out, such as a spec toolkit's. It is a directory under the package's `recipes/`, named by the token an adopter passes, holding two kinds of file:

- each `<stem>.knobs` file holds knob lines for the seam file of the same name;
- `unregister.list` names gates, one per line, that the registry drops.

A line opening with `#` is commentary in both, and any other file is not read. The packer places them ([§The packer](#the-packer)), and `init --recipe <name>` applies them.

**`--recipe` repeats, in application order**, and `--no-recipe` clears the set. A run passing neither re-applies the set the manifest records ([§The manifest](#the-manifest)), as a run passing no `--profile` re-applies the profile, and a run passing `--recipe` replaces it. `update` forwards both flags unchanged ([§update](#update)).

**Applying one changes two files `init` already writes, and adds none.** Each seam `init` writes is its kit template followed by each applied recipe's lines for it, in order. The gate-sdk seam has no template, so there the lines follow the placement's ([§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary)), and a line a recorded recipe carries is re-derived rather than kept. The registry ([§What init seeds](#what-init-seeds)) loses every gate an applied `unregister.list` names, and a name it does not carry is no finding. Both files are claimed before they are written, so a re-run with the same recipes rewrites what it wrote, and `diff` and `uninstall` read the recipe lines as `init`'s.

**Refused before any write, at exit 2**, the way an unknown profile is:

- a name the package's `recipes/` does not carry, the help naming those it does;
- a recipe `.knobs` file naming a seam file the selected kit set does not write, the help naming the profiles that write every one;
- a composed seam the knob grammar refuses, such as two recipes setting one scalar, naming the recipes that wrote into it.

**A kept file is reported, never merged into.** When you have edited a seam file or the registry, `init` keeps it ([§init](#init)). It prints each recipe line the kept seam lacks and each dropped gate the kept registry still registers, with the remedy: add them by hand, or pass `--force` to take `init`'s file. A kept file already carrying every line is reported as kept and nothing more. Merging into a file `init` does not own is the overwrite the ownership contract forbids.

`--dry-run` plans and prints the composed seams and the dropped gates through the same code.

**The lattice stays intact.** [§Profiles](#profiles)' monotonicity is a claim about the registries profiles write, and [§The consumer smoke](#the-consumer-smoke) asserts it over recipe-free installs. A recipe is consumer config applied after the profile, recorded beside it in the manifest, and changes no kit the profile vendors. A selection stands on the same footing ([§Selecting kits and gates](#selecting-kits-and-gates)).

**Recipes sit beside `payload/`, never inside it.** Every directory under `payload/` is read as a kit, one reserved name excepted ([§Profiles](#profiles)), so a second non-kit sibling would need a second exclusion in every derivation that walks it. The drop is data read from `unregister.list`, so no gate name enters the crate (`check-install-disposition`'s third assertion).

## Selecting kits and gates

A **selection** adjusts a profile per install. `--with-kit <kit>` adds a payload kit to the profile's kit set and `--without-kit <kit>` removes one. `--with-gate <gate>` registers a gate the derived registry does not carry, and `--without-gate <gate>` drops one from it. Each repeats and takes the `<flag>=<value>` form too, and `update` forwards them unchanged ([§update](#update)).

**The composition.** The vendored kit set is the profile's set, plus each `--with-kit`, less each `--without-kit`, in payload order. The registry is the derivation over that set ([§What init seeds](#what-init-seeds)), less every recipe drop and every `--without-gate`, plus every `--with-gate`, so an explicit `--with-gate` outranks a recipe's `unregister.list`. That set is what `init` vendors, declares in `GATE_SDK_KIT_DIRS`, records as `kits`, and hands `doctor` ([§doctor](#doctor)), so the toolchain floor is the selected set's. A selection is consumer config applied after the profile, on the recipes' footing: the lattice is a claim about the registries profiles write, asserted over selection-free installs ([§Profiles](#profiles)).

**The recorded selection.** `checkwright.lock` records it ([§The manifest](#the-manifest)). A run passing no selection flag re-applies it, a run passing any replaces it whole, and `--no-selection` clears it. So the command line that made an install states its whole selection, and no re-run half-merges two.

**Refused before any write, at exit 2**, each with a `help:` line naming what the package or tree does carry:

- a kit the payload does not carry;
- a `--without-kit` naming a kit every profile carries, which is gate-sdk: the runner, the hook generator and the registry every other kit's gates resolve through, so removing it leaves no battery;
- a `--with-gate` the registry's resolver would not resolve on this tree, the gates directory first and then each selected kit's `checks/`, or whose resolved declaration reads `# install: never` ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §The install disposition](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#the-install-disposition));
- a `--without-gate` that no selected kit's `checks/` ships and the gates directory does not carry, which is a typo rather than a choice;
- one name given to both `--with-kit` and `--without-kit`, or to both `--with-gate` and `--without-gate`;
- `--no-selection` beside any other selection flag.

A `--without-gate` naming a shipped gate the derived registry does not carry, such as an `on-surface` member, is no refusal: it is recorded, so the drop holds once the member is registered some other way. A kit removed on a re-run leaves `kits`, `GATE_SDK_KIT_DIRS` and the registry, and its files stay on disk and on the roster, since `init` never deletes ([§The manifest](#the-manifest)). `--dry-run` plans the selected kit set, the added and dropped gates and the recorded selection through the same code, and prints them. `init --help` lists the payload's kits beside its profiles and recipes.

**Replacing a gate is shadowing, and needs no flag.** A gate file of the same name in your gates directory, `<name>.sh` or `<name>.gate`, resolves before every kit's ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Layout and configuration](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#layout-and-configuration)). `init` never writes it, so it is yours across every re-run, `diff` and `uninstall` pass it by, and an upgrade's note names a kit gate that tightened under your shadow in its Tightened gates ([§The upgrade contract](#the-upgrade-contract)). A gate of your own under a new name is added with `--with-gate`, which the manifest records, so it survives the re-run a hand edit to `gates.list` would not.

## The install boundary

One part of an install must be written in whatever language the host already runs: the bootstrap that resolves, verifies and executes the gate binary. Everything else is **conditional install logic**. The **interpreter policy** puts all of it on the far side of that invoke, written once in Rust rather than twice, in POSIX sh and in the PowerShell a native Windows install needs. The policy binds the bootstrap's *shape*, not its existence: resolve the platform, place the matching binary, invoke it, which is small enough to write twice. The bootstrap below is the whole of the shell, and every verb is an arm of the binary it invokes. This section states the bootstrap's job, the disposition every install step carries and the test that assigns one, so a step's side of the line is read off a rule rather than argued per step.

**Two standing obligations** bind every unit that touches the install path: **add no new shell-only install step**, and **assume no POSIX shell on a host the PowerShell half serves**. Both are the interpreter policy's.

**The bootstrap's job is the whole of what is written twice:**

1. resolve the package's own payload directory;
2. resolve the host to its preferred Rust target triple, and that triple to its fallback where it has one;
3. read the payload's target roster and resolve each candidate's artifact and sidecar, preferred first, refusing a declared target whose pair is incomplete;
4. verify the artifact's SHA-256 against that sidecar, and where the candidate has a fallback, run it once with `--help`, passing to the fallback when it does not run;
5. execute the verified artifact, under one unconditional argv rule: a dashless leading token is prefixed with `--`, and everything after it is forwarded verbatim.

Step 5's rule is the only conditional shape either bootstrap carries, and it is unconditional in the sense that matters. It branches on the *shape* of the first token, never on which verb it is, so no verb table is kept in two languages. `checkwright init --profile starter` reaches the artifact as `--init --profile starter`; `checkwright --help` is forwarded unchanged. The binary therefore owns the verb roster ([§The verbs](#the-verbs)), and the two halves cannot disagree about a verb word.

**Every step's disposition takes one of three values.** The test that assigns one is *what the step needs that the binary cannot supply at that moment*:

- **`bootstrap`** — the step must precede the invoke, because the binary cannot select, verify or execute itself. The steps listed above, and nothing else.
- **`behind-invoke`** — conditional install logic, written once, in Rust. This is the default: the interpreter policy puts everything conditional on the far side of the invoke, so a step claiming `bootstrap` owes a reason drawn from the previous bullet and no other.
- **`retired`** — the step serves only a dependency the binary removes, so it is deleted rather than moved. `init`'s `jq` preflight was the worked case: nothing behind the invoke reads JSON with `jq`, because the crate reads it with `serde_json`.

**How the port oracle reads those three values — a stated contract a cut can cite.** The dispositions are a two-sided port disposition. `bootstrap` is the port's irreducible in the strict sense: something must run before the binary exists on the machine, and fetching and executing the first artifact cannot itself be that artifact. A file whose *whole* body is bootstrap steps declares `# no-port:` citing this paragraph, the only `no-port` cause `installer/` may carry. `behind-invoke` is a **port obligation**: a file carrying any such step stays `owed` in `--emit port-blockers --tree` until the step moves behind the invoke and the shell that ran it is deleted. `retired` steps are deleted, not declared. `installer/` carries the two bootstraps, each wholly bootstrap steps and each declaring `# no-port:` citing this paragraph, and nothing else. The `--pack-installer` arm's disposition is [§The packer](#the-packer)'s, not this section's.

Both halves of the disposition bind. Read with `bootstrap` silent, the one shell surface the interpreter policy sanctions would have no cause to declare on, and would read as owed forever. Read as saying only *when* a step runs and not *whether* it ports, the rule would void its own words for `behind-invoke`, "written once, in Rust", which is a port commitment.

### Parity between the two bootstraps

**The two bootstraps are hand-kept, and parity is held by running, not by generation.** Each half is authored in its own language against the five steps above, and a per-bootstrap install-smoke leg is the oracle that holds them equal. A leg is named `install-smoke-<bootstrap>-<platform>`, so its first segment is the bootstrap it drives, and the count read off the names is two bootstraps, `sh` and `pwsh`. The platform segments move with the platform declaration. **No other leg substitutes for the `pwsh` one**, because every other leg drives the `sh` bootstrap.

A leg asserts two distinct things. **Bootstrap parity** is that the two halves answer the five steps the same way. **Payload coverage** is that a whole `checkwright init` completes through that bootstrap. The hand-kept-parity rule guards drift between the two bootstraps, and running the payload end to end adds coverage, not parity. A new leg states which of the two it adds.

**The running oracle cannot reach one region, so a static check complements it.** The PowerShell leg runs once per declared Windows triple, on that triple's runner only. `Get-HostTarget`'s `linux/x64` and `linux/arm64` arms are therefore executed by no run this repository buys, and no run it could buy today would reach them. `check-install-platforms` asserts each detector's emitted triple set statically, covering exactly the region the running oracle cannot reach and leaving the rest to the legs. It generates neither half and retires no leg. It complements the legs rather than contesting them, because running tells you *that* the halves differ, never *where*.

**What a reader compares when the two legs disagree.** With two hand-kept halves, a red on one leg beside a green on the other is routine. The comparison therefore has a stated order: the five steps in sequence, each with the observable that settles it. A session arriving at a divergence walks it rather than diffing two languages:

| step | what to compare | the observable that settles it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 payload directory | the resolved package root, after the symlink chain | the path each half prints when the payload is absent |
| 2 host triple | the triple each half maps this host to, and its fallback | one half's empty string against the other's triple, or the two naming different fallbacks |
| 3 selection | which of the four outcomes each half reached | unrostered vs. verify vs. broken payload vs. does not run, and which candidate each half took, by message and remedy, never the exit status alone |
| 4 digest | the hex compared, and its case | a mismatch on identical bytes is a case fold, not a corrupt artifact |
| 5 execution | the argv the artifact actually received | the binary's own usage refusal, which echoes what it was handed |

Step 4 is the row that most often reads as a defect and is not one. `Get-FileHash` returns upper-case hex where the sidecar carries `sha256sum`'s lower case, so the halves agree on the digest and differ only in its spelling. Step 3 is the row where the exit status alone misleads. Three of the four outcomes refuse, so a reader comparing statuses sees one answer where an adopter is owed three. They are a platform they can do nothing about, a payload they fix by re-downloading, and a binary that does not run on their host, which they report. Compare the message and the remedy, the same economy the truth table in [§The consumer smoke](#the-consumer-smoke) buys.

**Two host assumptions this bootstrap rests on are measured, not assumed.** Both were measured on a native Windows runner. `[[ -x ]]` **holds** on a freshly `chmod +x`'d shebang script, which executes directly despite `core.filemode=false`. It also **holds** on npm's extension-less bin shim, written mode `-rwxr-xr-x` beside its `.cmd` and `.ps1` siblings. So neither `-x` test needs a Windows special case, and neither bootstrap carries a mode-detection branch. They are recorded because the answer cost a runner to buy, and a reader meeting either test would otherwise ask again.

**One declaration generating both halves is refused.** At five steps, a generator is a third artifact to maintain (a template language, a freshness gate and a projection-roster row) for a surface small enough to write twice by design. A generated twin still needs its platform leg to prove it runs, so the generator buys no oracle the legs do not already supply. Drift between hand-kept halves is a *real* cost, and the leg is what turns it into a red run rather than a reading.

### What runs behind the invoke

**Step 5 is *execute*, not *install*.** The tracked copy of the binary in the consumer's gates directory is an install artifact with ownership semantics: claimed against the manifest, carried in `files[]`, removed by `uninstall`. Placing it is therefore conditional install logic, and sits `behind-invoke`. The bootstrap runs the artifact **in place, out of the payload**, where step 4 has just verified it; a copy to a scratch path to run it would be a copy with no reader. The interpreter policy's "place the matching binary" so means *make the binary runnable*.

**The generation step spawns only the binary `init` placed.** The binary's own `--emit git-hooks --write` and `--emit graph` arms generate the hooks and the coupling graph ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §gen-pre-commit](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#gen-pre-commit)). `check-graph` is `install: zero-config`, so a fresh consumer's day-one battery holds the generated hook against its emission, and the hook must exist at install: the step cannot be dropped. `init` runs the artifact it just placed at the consumer's root, with `GATE_SDK_ROOT` in the child's environment naming the root-vendored `gate-sdk` directory, as the front-end would export it ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Layout and configuration](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#layout-and-configuration)). The front-end's only other duties, changing to the root and locating the binary, are ones `init` already holds. So `init` spawns only `git` and that binary, never `bash`. The bootstrap, which the standing "assume no POSIX shell" obligation binds, spawns nothing but a verified artifact: the one it executes, and on Linux the preferred one it asks to run.

**`--install <op>` is the seam both bootstraps call**, specified so the two calls are byte-identical. It is a non-gate arm of the binary ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §The non-gate arm](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#the-non-gate-arm)), and it reads no kit config and no knob. Its caller is a bootstrap that may not be a POSIX shell at all, and a knob read would tie the call's meaning to whatever knob files the working directory holds, which neither bootstrap controls. So **every value the arm needs arrives as argv**.

- **Grammar.** `--install <op> [--<key> <value>]…`, `<op>` from a closed set, an unknown `<op>` or an unknown key exiting 2.
- **Channels, because the caller is a program in two languages.** *stdout* is a wire: one record per line, tab-separated, `<verb><TAB><field>…`. *stderr* is the adopter-facing report.
- **Exit status.** `0` performed — or, under `--dry-run`, planned; `1` an adopter-actionable refusal; `2` usage or harness error, on [gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Fail-closed contract](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#fail-closed-contract)'s terms.
- **`--dry-run` is owed by every mutating op**, on [§The verbs](#the-verbs)' existing classifier: print the plan, write nothing, exit 0.

The family carries two ops, and neither produces a `1`. `place-artifact`'s only failures are a bad argv and a write it could not make, and `queue-source` reads and writes nothing, so both refuse at `2`. The status is specified on the family rather than per op, so a later op that *can* refuse something the adopter can act on has a status to refuse with.

**`queue-source` is a read op, and the family's grammar is what it costs.** `--install queue-source --payload <dir> --kits <kit>[,<kit>…]` answers which template a kit set's queue is seeded from, the derivation [§What init seeds](#what-init-seeds) states. It emits `queue-source<TAB><path>` when one is owed and **an empty wire** when none is, so a caller's whole reading is *nonempty means owed*, with no field to interpret. It exists because the derivation has a second reader outside the package. The consumer smoke asserts init's queue post-condition and must not carry a second copy of the rule, so it reads this one across the package boundary ([§The consumer smoke](#the-consumer-smoke)). The op takes this family's grammar, channels and exit statuses rather than a contract of its own, so the smoke calls the seam the bootstraps already call.

**The adopter verbs are not ops of this family, because their output channels conflict.** This family specifies stdout as a *wire*: tab-separated records, one per line. `init`'s stdout carries the adopter-facing follow-up block, whose grammar [§init](#init) states and whose reader is the consumer smoke's follow-up arm. One of the two contracts would have had to yield. So the verbs are top-level `--`-prefixed arms, resolved before the registry lookup ([§The verbs](#the-verbs)), and this family keeps its wire for a caller that is a program in two languages. The line is not where a step *runs*, since every verb is behind the invoke exactly as an op is; it is which **channel contract** its output answers to.

### Hosts refused at the bootstrap

**A host that cannot run the verified binary is refused at the bootstrap.** Every step of an install sits behind the invoke, so on such a host an install has no code path at all. Proceeding would be **not a smaller battery but a silent non-install**. Three such hosts exist, two met at selection and one at verification ([§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary)):

- **An unrostered host is refused, naming the platform.** There is no adopter action, and saying so beats writing a tree whose battery cannot run.
- **A host on which the preferred artifact does not run, with no fallback rostered, is refused**, naming the triple. It has no adopter action either, and the remedy asks for a report of the host, the triple and the release.
- **A POSIX host carrying neither `sha256sum` nor `shasum` is refused** rather than served an unverified artifact. Step 4 of the bootstrap is irreducible: a host that cannot hash cannot verify, and verifying before executing is the whole of the integrity claim. On the PowerShell half the branch is vacuous, since `Get-FileHash` is always there.

Both hosts once **proceeded**, omitting the compiled gates and declaring the omission in the consumer's `gates.list`. That kept no battery alive: every registered member dispatches to the binary, so an artifact-less install had no live member, and its battery refused. The refusal is the honest form of what those hosts were already getting.

**Nothing past step 5 needs an external hasher.** The binary hashes in-process. Only the bootstrap's own step 4 still needs one, because it cannot use the binary to verify the binary.

## The gate binary

A gate whose implementation is a compiled subcommand needs that binary on disk before it can run, and `init` puts it there. Selecting and verifying it is the **bootstrap's** job, because the binary cannot select itself; placing it in the consumer's tree is `init`'s, behind the invoke. Nothing builds and nothing fetches. Selection and verification sit inside the irreducible bootstrap the vendoring ruling leaves outside the binary ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Porting a gate to the binary substrate](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#porting-a-gate-to-the-binary-substrate)), and each is small enough to be written twice, in POSIX sh and in PowerShell. The section follows the bootstrap's order: platform resolution, selection, verification, then placement behind the invoke.

### Platform resolution

**Platform resolution is derived and never stored.** In the **POSIX sh** half, `target_of_host()` maps `uname -s` and `uname -m` to one Rust target triple, or to the empty string on a host that maps to none. It runs once per invocation, before anything else. The result stays a local. A stored copy would be a second source for a fact the host already answers, stale the first time a vendored tree moves between machines, and a vendored tree is shared by construction. It reads two fields rather than `uname -a`: they are the smallest input that answers the question, and a PowerShell half can answer them without parsing prose. Nothing reads the kernel version, so nothing collects it. The Windows family takes its architecture from elsewhere, and the PowerShell half answers from its own runtime; both follow below.

**Each half's mapped triple set is machine-read, so each half's shape is pinned.** The `case` and `switch` arms own the triples. A roster comment beside them would be a second copy, exactly the drift `check-install-platforms` exists to catch. So the gate reads the arms, and their shape is stated here:

- **POSIX sh** — inside the bodies of `target_of_host` and of `fallback_of_target`, the fallback map, every mapped triple is the **sole single-quoted operand of a `printf`** and appears nowhere else in the function. The fallback map's case patterns name the preferred triples unquoted.
- **PowerShell** — inside the bodies of `Get-HostTarget` and of `Get-FallbackTarget`, its twin, every mapped triple is the **sole single-quoted operand of a `return`**, and the empty `return ''` is the no-mapping arm rather than a triple. The `switch` patterns are also single-quoted, which is why the pin is on `return` and not on quoting.

A half's emitted set is the union of both its functions' operands. Each body is bounded by its own closing brace at column 0. Every way that extraction can degrade is **fail-closed (exit 2)**, because this arm's failure mode is silence: the named function absent or renamed, its body unbounded, zero triples extracted, or either file unreadable. Each is a check that could not run, never a pass. An extraction that silently degrades to nothing is the one way a lockstep assertion reports agreement it never tested.

**The map answers "which published artifact fits this host", which is why a MinGW, MSYS or Cygwin `uname` maps to `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`.** Those `uname` strings report the *shell environment*, not the toolchain that built the artifact the adopter is about to receive. The measured runner answers `MINGW64_NT-10.0-26100`/`x86_64`. The Windows build leg publishes what that host's own `rustc` reports as its host triple, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. That triple is on `native/targets.list`, joined on a run that produced and exercised its artifact ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload)), so `select_artifact`'s roster comparison passes for these hosts.

**On the Windows family the architecture is the OS's, read from the registry, because `uname -m` there names the POSIX runtime's.** The MSYS runtime Git for Windows ships is built for x86_64 only, and runs emulated on an ARM64 host. Its `uname` reports the architecture that emulated process is shown, so an ARM64 host answers `MINGW64_NT-*`/`x86_64` exactly as an x64 one does, and `PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE` in the process environment is `AMD64` too. `host_arch()` therefore reads `PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE` from `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment`, the value the system environment is built from. It reads it through the runtime's `/proc/registry`, with no child process. `ARM64` there answers `aarch64`, which the `MINGW*`/`MSYS*`/`CYGWIN*` arm maps to `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc`. Any other value, or no readable value, leaves `uname -m`'s answer standing, so an x64 host keeps its triple. An ARM64 host is so served the native ARM64 artifact rather than the x64 one under emulation. While a triple is held, the same resolution refuses the host rather than falling back to emulation, since no run has measured the x64 artifact there.

**The PowerShell half reads the runtime instead, and reaches the same triple.** It asks the .NET runtime for the OS platform and architecture rather than shelling out to `uname`. The host this half exists for need carry no POSIX shell, so it need carry no `uname`. On a native Windows x64 host it resolves `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, as the POSIX half's `MINGW*`/`MSYS*`/`CYGWIN*` arm does, for the same reason. On a native Windows ARM64 host the runtime answers `Arm64`. The half then resolves `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc`, the triple the POSIX half reaches through the registry. The `switch` matches case-insensitively, so the fallback's `ARM64` spelling reaches the same arm. Both triples are rostered, so selection passes on either host. Each half's ARM64 arm has a running witness on the arm64 entry of `install-smoke-pwsh-windows`: its POSIX-bootstrap step, which installs the lattice minimum through `installer/bin/checkwright.sh`, for the POSIX half, and its PowerShell steps for this one.

**Neither input answers the libc question, and the loader does.** A Linux host maps to the glibc triple, and that triple names the static musl triple of the same architecture as its fallback. The glibc artifact runs only on a glibc at or above the floor it was linked against, while the static one runs on any Linux kernel at its floor. So the bootstrap asks the verified glibc artifact to run, and takes the fallback when it cannot ([§Selection](#selection)). `uname -s`/`uname -m` and .NET's `OSPlatform`/`OSArchitecture` still answer everything the map needs, and neither bootstrap reads a C library's name or version. A version comparison would spell each glibc floor a second time in each bootstrap, where the install page's Minimum cell and the build body's measurement are the owners, and it would re-ask a question the loader answers exactly. Making musl every host's artifact, with glibc on explicit request, is refused too: it needs an adopter-facing selector nobody would set, and it publishes a glibc build no install takes.

### Selection

**Selection has four outcomes, only one of which proceeds, and collapsing any two is a defect.** The payload carries the target roster verbatim beside the artifacts ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload)), and the bootstrap reads it rather than inferring support from a directory's presence. The host's candidates are its preferred triple and, on Linux, that triple's fallback ([§Platform resolution](#platform-resolution)):

| the host's candidates | the payload holds | outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| none in the roster | — | **refuse**: this platform is not in the support roster; there is no adopter action |
| a rostered one | nothing, or half its pair | **refuse**: the payload is broken |
| a rostered one, verified | its pair, and it runs or has no fallback | execute |
| a rostered one with a fallback, verified | its pair, and it does not run, with no rostered fallback | **refuse**: this binary does not run on this host; there is no adopter action |

**A candidate that does not run passes to its fallback, and no refusal does.** A preferred triple the roster lacks, which is a held one, and a verified preferred artifact that does not run both pass to the fallback. A broken pair and a digest mismatch refuse, because they are defects in what was published, and serving the fallback would hide them behind a working install. The probe runs `<artifact> --help` once with its output discarded; a start failure or a non-zero exit is "does not run", which is what a glibc below the artifact's floor or a host with no glibc loader produces. In the PowerShell half a start failure is the exception `&` throws, caught, and a non-zero `$LASTEXITCODE`. The probe runs only after verification, so nothing unverified is executed, and only where a fallback exists, so no other host runs its artifact twice.

**Every refusal here names what the host was detected AS.** The message carries the detected `<os>/<arch>`. Without it, neither an adopter nor a maintainer reading their bug report can tell an unsupported architecture from a `uname` that answered nothing. A refusal message is a documented surface: [gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Fail-closed contract](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#fail-closed-contract)'s rule for the wrapper class, applied to this boundary's refusals.

The four stay told apart by **message and remedy**, never by exit status alone, because an undeclared host, a broken payload and a binary that does not run here are different answers to an adopter. The broken-payload row is the whole reason the roster is read. Without it, the bootstrap cannot tell a platform never committed to from one committed to whose artifact went missing, and reading the second as the first turns a publisher defect into a silently smaller green battery. A payload assembled with no artifacts at all carries no `artifact/` directory, so it reads as the first row, never as a payload whose every target went missing. Both bootstraps owe all four rows and answer them identically; why the first row refuses rather than omitting is [§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary)'s.

**"Its binary" is the one regular file in the target's directory not ending in `.sha256`**, and "its sidecar" is that name plus `.sha256`; zero or several such files is the broken-payload row. The POSIX half counts them with a glob over the directory rather than with `find`, so no primary can disagree between GNU and BSD userlands. The glob skips dotfiles, so a stray dotfile beside the binary is not a second artifact.

**Every row of the selection table runs under an oracle**, split across [§The consumer smoke](#the-consumer-smoke)'s arms by which install can show it. The **verify-then-write** row is the main loop's, on every profile, because the payload it packs carries a binary that run built. The **unrostered-host** row is the binary-less leg's and the artifact arm's undeclared-host leg's. The **broken-payload** row is the artifact arm's alone, against a payload it mutated after extraction. The **does-not-run** row, and the execute row's fallback path, are the artifact arm's no-fallback and falls-back cases, which run wherever the hand-off carries a foreign-architecture preferred artifact.

**The registry's `# omitted:` class is gate-sdk's, not an install outcome.** `# omitted: <name> <reason>` is a comment line the runner strips from the live set and reports beside its summary ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §run-gates](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#run-gates)). It is **reason-agnostic**: any consumer may omit a member for a cause of their own. `init` once wrote it in place of a member it could not install, with two install-time reason tokens for two remedies. Both tokens are retired, because an unrostered host and a hasher-less host are refused before an install begins ([§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary)), so an install that happens at all installs the whole starting roster. Retiring them did not narrow the class: narrowing it would publish an installer decision as a kit narrowing. `doctor` reports whatever reason it finds and invents no remedy for it ([§doctor](#doctor)).

### Verification

**The digest is verified before anything is executed.** The bootstrap computes the artifact's SHA-256, compares it against the sidecar that travelled with it, and only then runs it. The ordering is the whole of it: a consumer who cannot read the gate has nothing else standing between them and a substituted binary. A mismatch refuses: never a warning, never a run.

`sha256sum` is tried first, then `shasum -a 256`, because stock macOS ships the second and not the first. When **neither** resolves, the bootstrap **refuses**: nothing unverified is ever executed, and no path here skips the check. The placement `init` performs behind the invoke verifies without an external hasher, because the binary hashes in-process.

**The PowerShell half has no hasher resolution, by design.** PowerShell carries `Get-FileHash`, so that half has no hasher to choose, no `sha256sum`/`shasum` fallback and no refusal to reach. This is the one step where the twin is simpler than the original rather than parallel to it; a reader holding the halves side by side should not read the missing branch as a defect. Its one asymmetry is spelling, not logic: `Get-FileHash` returns upper-case hex against a lower-case sidecar, so that half folds case before comparing.

**The artifact is the one path the changed-file protection skips, which makes the digest actionable.** Everywhere else `init` writes, a file whose recorded hash disagrees with the tree is yours, so it is reported and left alone ([§init](#init)). A compiled artifact has no version you authored. A binary that fails the recorded digest is corrupt or substituted, never edited. So `init` rewrites it from the payload copy it just verified rather than reporting it as changed, and `uninstall` removes it rather than keeping it ([§uninstall](#uninstall)). Without this exemption, diagnosis and remedy would come apart. [§doctor](#doctor) reports the mismatch and names a re-run as the fix, and a re-run that classified the binary as yours would leave it in place forever. `--force` is therefore never needed here and means nothing extra. The exemption covers the artifact path alone; the config seam written beside it is a file you do edit, and it is claimed like everything else.
