First-come alone is not a sample but an accident, and the accident has a direction: a first path that is a `.md` shows the end-of-line-shaped case and never the one that kills it. The artifact row is the discriminating case precisely because git classifies its blob binary and converts a binary blob under no configuration.

Where the manifest records no artifact key, the second sample is absent and the report says so rather than printing a blank. So are the other two ways it can fail to resolve: a manifest recording an artifact no config seam names a path for, and an artifact row that is not in the disagreeing set. No arm of this smoke produces the first of those three, since an install that ran placed a verified artifact. It is kept as the report's own fail-soft rather than as a case with a witness.

The third is the **witness for the exit-2 verdict**: the first disagreeing entry whose `want` or `got` failed the operand shape test. It is carried out of the loop as the same `<path><TAB><want><TAB><got>` tuple every disagreement is recorded as. It is appended last and deduplicated **on the whole tuple**, so a run cannot exit 2 on an entry whose *bytes* this report did not print. The artifact row above it dedups on the same predicate for the same reason. A path is what a reader looks a row up by, and bytes are what the verdict was computed on, so a path match is no evidence that the two rows are one row.

Whether the witness coincides with a sample already chosen is therefore a **check this report performs and prints**, never a claim it makes. It has three outcomes:

- **byte-equal**: the witness row is one of the samples already chosen. The report says so, in the shape the artifact row already uses, because the reader's question is the same one ("is this the row the verdict is about?") and a silent collapse answers it wrongly.
- **path-equal, bytes differ**: both blocks are printed, the witness block labelled as the row the verdict below is computed from. The report states plainly that two decompositions of one recorded entry disagree, which is a statement about **this harness** and not about the consumer's tree.
- **absent**: the witness row is not among the samples, and joins them.

A path-only predicate cannot tell the middle outcome from the first. The header states **how many** disagreements failed the shape test, and that count says whether the one printed witness row is representative. One malformed entry out of hundreds is a statement about that path, and all of them a statement about the capture step every entry runs through. Those two readings send a reader to different places.

> **A run-wide verdict states which entry earned it, or it is not readable.** Where an arm reports a bounded sample and decides on an unbounded scan, the deciding entry joins the sample. A flag recording only *that* something tripped it hands the reader a verdict and withholds its subject.

The witness is the first such entry rather than every one, on the sampler's own standing ground: the report is a bounded sample by design, and a report that prints hundreds of rows is a report nobody reads. Keeping the other two members is deliberate. They answer different questions from the verdict's row, and the artifact row in particular is the discriminating case the binary-conversion argument above rests on. A sampler narrowed to the verdict's row alone would buy the verdict's legibility with the discriminating case.

**Six values per sampled path, and the truth table that reads them.** Each is labelled and printed plain. Each is rendered twice, by `printf '%q'` and as an **octet dump** beside its own length, and judged by the decomposed shape test, with the call that produced it and that call's standard error. **Two of the six are the operands the failing comparison used, printed out of the variables it read; the other four are re-reads.** That split is the block's whole architecture. A value that reaches the comparison mangled and re-reads clean is invisible to a report that asks again.

- **`want`**: **held.** `files[P]` as the arm's own loop holds it. The loop reads the manifest line whole with `IFS= read -r line` and takes `want` off it by parameter expansion, so this is what that split produced and one of the two values the failing comparison used. It is deliberately **not** re-read through a second channel.
- **`got`**: **held.** The line the arm's single `git hash-object --stdin-paths` child answered for `$C/P`, paired with P by its position among the entries the loop hashed and carried out of the loop on the failure branch. It is the comparison's other operand, not a description of one.
- **`reread`**: a re-read. `git hash-object -- "$C/P"`, the one-file call, run at report time from the same working directory as the batch. A held value and a re-read of the same call carry two labels, so they can never be read as one thing.
- **`own`**: a re-read. `git -C "$C" hash-object -- "P"`, the same command in the repository context the installer's own recorded-hash helper runs in, which is the only thing the two call sites differ by.
- **`raw`**: a re-read. `git hash-object --no-filters -- "$C/P"`, the file's bytes with the attribute mechanism removed. `--no-filters` ignores attributes entirely, so this value depends on no repository, which makes it the fixed point the other re-reads are measured against.
- **`wantalt`**: a re-read, and the only one that reads the *manifest*. `jq -r --arg p "P" '.files[$p]' "$LOCK"`: the same key out of the same lock, straight into a command substitution. `want` arrives through a `jq` line render, a tab delimiter and a `read` split, any of which could mangle it, and this control shares none of them. `want != wantalt` places the defect in that pipeline and the two octet dumps name the byte. `want == wantalt` with identical dumps exonerates the pipeline and leaves the matcher as the remaining subject.

*`wantalt` does not discriminate a line terminator.* A single-value capture holds exactly one terminator and the command substitution always consumes it. It comes back clean whichever end of the stream put a trailing carriage return there, so it cannot separate the producer from the channel.

*A held value's `call` line states where the value was read from, and is permitted to state nothing more.* It names the variable and the read that assigned it. It may **not** assert that the value is the one the failing comparison used and not a second read of it. That is an identity between two decompositions of one recorded string, and no call site can check it. An unverifiable assertion there is worse than none: the `call` line is what licenses a reader to treat the report as adjudicating the verdict, so it would convert a live defect into positive evidence of health. The identity claim lives in the coincidence outcome above, where it is checked. A re-read value's `call` line prints the command that produced the value, which a reader can re-run, and asserts nothing beyond that.

**The manifest line is read whole and split in the shell, which is what makes the stream itself observable.** The loop reads with `IFS= read -r line` and derives `path` and `want` by parameter expansion. The bytes the channel delivered so exist in a variable before anything splits them. Reading with `IFS=$'\t' read -r path want` makes the split the same operation that consumes the evidence. There is then no point at which the delivered line is a value the report could print.

*The split is also less normalizing than the read it replaces.* Tab is an **IFS whitespace** character, so `IFS=$'\t' read` collapses runs of tabs and strips trailing ones: on the line `a\t\tb\t` the read yields `path=a want=b` while the expansion yields `path=a want=$'\tb\t'`. On the two-field, single-tab line `jq -r '"\(.key)\t\(.value)"'` emits, the two agree byte for byte. That holds on a CR-terminated line, where neither strips the CR, and on a path carrying a space, which `IFS=$'\t'` leaves alone. Where they differ is on an **anomalous** line, and there the read normalizes the anomaly away before anything can observe it. That is the anti-normalization rule below, reached at the read.

**Two raw stream lines, printed once per report rather than once per sampled path**: the **first line of the stream**, whatever it is, and the **raw line of the first disagreeing entry**. They answer different questions. The first says whether the channel delivers CRLF at all and is unconditional on any comparison, the cheapest possible statement about the stream. The second says whether *this* entry's bytes are what the verdict claims, the question the verdict is actually about. They are facts about the run and not about a path, so they sit outside the per-path block, as the worktree and config witnesses do. They ride as **named operands** rather than being re-read, because a value re-read is a second observation and cannot testify about the first. Their `tests` line is not a finding: a raw line is a path, a tab and a hash, so it fails the hash shape test by construction. The `octets` line, produced through no construct that could normalize, is what they are printed for.

Two values cannot separate *one side filtered* from *the bytes changed*, and no number of re-reads alone can separate either from *the comparison was handed something else*. Six can, and the reading rule lives here rather than with whoever reads the log next. The first three rows read the **hashing**, the next two read the **comparison**, and the sixth is the catch-all on any value's shape. The next three read the **instrument** rather than the operand, and the last three read the **channel** (the stream, the split, and this harness's own record of the entry):

| observation | reading |
| --- | --- |
| `want == own == raw` and `reread != raw` | the read side's context applies a filter the write side's does not; the defect is at `run-smoke.sh`'s call site and the two-call-site narrowing is confirmed |
| `want == own == reread` | the hashes agree and the arm could not have failed on this path — the disagreement is in the comparison, not in the hashing (whether they also equal `raw` says only *why* they agree: equal, no context filters at all; unequal, both contexts filter identically — neither changes the reading) |
| `own == reread == raw` and `want != raw` | the bytes on disk are not the bytes `init` hashed; the porcelain below and the artifact control say which |
| `got != reread` | the batch's answer for this path is not what the one-file call gives now. Either the value was mangled when the batch was captured or read back, or the batch filed another path's answer here. The two octet dumps name the byte and its position, and a `got` that is a well-formed hash of a different path is the second case |
| `want == got`, byte-equal, both held | the comparison received two equal values and reported them unequal, which bash cannot do — so a pairing is wrong. Either `bad_hash` associated one entry's `want` with another entry's `got`, or the batch answer was paired off by one. Read the sampled path against the loop's own echo order. The count refusal rules out a short answer, not a reordered one |
| any of the six fails the shape test | a stray byte, a truncation or a refusal will each do it and the value is then not a hash; `len` names a truncation outright, the octet dump shows a stray byte, and the captured standard error names the refusal. Read it against the row below first, which is the one case where that reading does not hold. The arm acts on this row too, and that is the one row it acts on: a refused operand makes the run **exit 2** rather than 1. Read it with the header's count: **one** entry failing the shape test is a statement about the sampled path, **all** of them a statement about the capture step every entry runs through |
| `shape` fails while `len40` and `class` are both clean | two matchers in one shell disagree about one variable — the ERE engine or its locale is the subject, not the value; the operand is a hash and the harness refused it anyway |
| `%q` renders bare while `octets` shows a byte outside `0-9a-f` | `printf '%q'` is not a byte rendering on this host, so **every** "bare rendering" reading is weakened to what quoting alone establishes; re-read one against the octet dump before citing it |
| `want != wantalt` | the manifest pipeline mangles between the lock and the comparison — the `jq` line render, the tab, or `read`'s splitting; the two octet dumps name the byte and the position |
| the first stream line's `octets` end `0d 0a`, or `0d` once the newline is stripped | the channel delivers CRLF into the manifest stream at all, before any entry is compared. This is the one row that reads the **stream** rather than a value, and the decision rule below names what each dump selects |
| the disagreeing entry's raw line against that same entry's `want` | separates *the carriage return arrived in the stream* from *it was introduced at the split*: a `0d` in both puts it in the stream, a `0d` in `want` alone puts it at or after the split, and neither carrying one puts the fault in the verdict's decomposition rather than in the value |
| the coincidence outcome reads **path-equal, bytes differ** | the report's witness row and an earlier sample carry one path and two different tuples, so one recorded entry has two decompositions and they disagree. The subject is **this harness**, not the consumer, and the two blocks printed under that path are the evidence. What it suspends is bounded, because the disagreeing blocks are exactly the ones carried in through the trailing `${bad_hash[@]+…}` operand: every row read off a **sample block's** `want` or `got` is suspended for that run, while `stream1`, `badline`, the witness row and the header's counts arrive as scalar operands and `reread`, `own`, `raw` and `wantalt` are commands the report re-runs — none of those is implicated, and a sample whose probes returned a hash at all proves its own path field crossed intact. A repair chosen off the unimplicated operands is sound; one chosen off a sample block's tuple is not |

The instrument rows exist because a report rendered through one subsystem cannot adjudicate a disagreement between two, and every row above them reads the operand.

**Two renderings, and only one of them can carry a byte claim.** `printf '%q'` is a **shell-quoting** renderer: it emits a string bash can re-read to the same value. For the class that motivated it, a value carrying a trailing carriage return that compares unequal and *prints* equal, quoting and byte-exactness coincide as `$'…\r'`. That is why the rendering is neither decoration nor optional. They are still not the same property. A rendering that quotes nothing establishes that bash's formatter found nothing worth quoting, and **not** that the value holds forty bytes drawn from `0-9a-f`. The `octets` line carries the byte claim: the value's bytes in hexadecimal, produced by piping it through `od` with no interpretation. It passes through no construct that could itself normalize: no `echo`, whose escape handling is shell-dependent, and no re-quoting. Both are printed, because a disagreement between them is itself a finding and because earlier `%q`-only readings stay reproducible against a later run.

**The shape test's parts print beside the value they judged, and the class half deliberately uses a different matcher.** The `tests` line carries `len40`, whether `${#v}` is exactly 40, then `class` and `shape`. `class` is computed by `leftover="${v//[0-9a-f]/}"`, the residue after deleting every acceptable character, which is exactly the offending set. Where it is non-empty the line names that residue and the **zero-based index of the first offending character**, so the reader gets a position and not only a set. `shape` is the composite `[[ "$v" =~ ^[0-9a-f]{40}$ ]]` verdict itself. The class test is a parameter expansion over a **glob bracket expression**, while the composite is an **ERE** evaluated by the platform's `regcomp`/`regexec`. They are two independent implementations of "is this character acceptable", and that is the whole mechanism. Using `=~` for the decomposition would inherit whatever the composite suffers and print an agreement that means nothing.

*The decomposition is an observation and never a verdict, and that refusal is load-bearing.* The composite `=~` stays the thing that selects the exit code. Moving the decider onto the decomposed test would green a leg on a **hypothesis**, that the ERE engine is the faulty subsystem, and it would destroy the disagreement that is the entire evidence. It is the trap the anti-normalization rule below closes, reached from a new direction: normalizing the operand and swapping in a matcher that happens to accept it are one move under two spellings.

**A refused operand is a precondition of this harness, so it exits 2, never the manifest verdict at 1.** `starter: N of N manifest entries disagree with the tree` at exit 1 is a statement *about the consumer*: the tree `init` wrote does not match what `init` recorded. If a value reached the comparison malformed, nothing about the consumer has been established. The honest code is then the harness-precondition one, which every preflight refusal in this script already takes, reached one step inward to the arm's own operands. **The 2 rests on a second ground as well.** A matcher that refuses a well-formed hash is a harness precondition every bit as much as a mangled operand is, and likewise no finding about the consumer's tree. The code is the same 2 in both cases, and the refusal below is what tells the two apart.

The arm therefore shape-tests both operands on the failure branch. After the report has printed, it routes a refused one through `blocked` at exit 2 instead of `fail` at exit 1. **It fires after the report, not at the first bad value**, because diagnosing that value is exactly what the report exists for, and refusing early would trade the report for the verdict. The witness sample above is what makes the report contain the refusal's subject. The refusal itself names that subject: the path, which of `want` and `got` the shape test refused (or both), how many disagreements it refused, and the **decomposed verdict for each refused operand**. The verdict is so readable from the last line alone.

*It reports the test's verdict, and never declares the operand malformed.* Those are different claims, and the second can be false while the first is true. Where the decomposition reads `len40=yes class=clean`, the operand **is** a hash, and this harness's matcher refused one. The last line carries the decomposition so its reader can tell those apart. The shape row above is not redundant: that row tells a **reader** what a refusal means, and this makes the **arm** act on it. A report a human reads and a verdict a suite reads are two consumers, and deleting either for the other is the mistake.

*Who reads the 2, and the honest limit that comes with it.* The verdict class is read by CI's job verdict and by a human reading the log, and by **nothing else**. `scripts/evidence-config.knobs` gives the `installer_smoke` suite the `parse-smoke-log` parser, and that custom-parser path never references the process status it is handed. The evidence row is derived from the log's arm headers alone, so **exit 1 and exit 2 are indistinguishable to it**. The distinction is real and invisible to `--run-validate`'s evidence, and nothing above depends on it.

**What the arm must not do is normalize.** Trimming the operands to their 40-hex core before comparing would turn a mangled-operand red green, and it is the one repair this arm is closed to. It would make the instrument accept a broken producer silently: enforcement inverted, the defect absorbed by the detector. It would also make a later green unreadable as evidence, unable to distinguish *the tree matches* from *the tree matches once the arm discards whatever reached it*. The refusal above is the honest form of the same observation: an operand that is not a hash stops the run instead of being repaired into one.

*The same rule reaches the report's own **decompositions**.* Where two independent readings of one recorded string disagree, the disagreement is printed and named, never resolved in favour of either. One decomposition helper that both the report and the verdict call is **refused**, on the ground the shape test's own two matchers stand on: two independent implementations reading one variable make their disagreement observable instead of absorbed. Normalizing an operand and unifying the readings that disagree about it are one move under two spellings.

*And it reaches the **read**.* A read that collapses tab runs and strips trailing tabs deletes a class of anomaly before any probe can see it, so the arm would be normalizing its own input while refusing to normalize its operands. The loop therefore reads the line whole and splits it in the shell, as stated above.

*The one byte the read does own is the line **terminator**.* A terminator is a property of the channel a record travels over and not of the record. A line delivered CRLF carries a byte that was never in the manifest, and the values on that line are hashes `init` took from `git`, which cannot end in one. The loop therefore drops **one** trailing carriage return before it splits. It keeps the raw line unstripped for the two evidence operands the report prints, and **declares the count** it dropped, on the green path as well as the red. That declaration separates this from the repair the rule closes the arm to. Trimming an operand to its 40-hex core deletes the evidence and reports nothing. A per-line terminator strip that prints how many of how many lines carried one leaves a value that genuinely ended in a carriage return visible, as a count that does not fit the channel's shape. Exactly one is taken, so a doubled carriage return still reaches the shape test and still fails it.

**The terminator handling has one owner.** `$( )` consumes exactly the last terminator while `<( )` consumes none, so a CRLF stream reaches every multi-line reader of a `jq` stream and no single-value capture. A `mapfile -t` splits on newline alone, so on a CRLF stream every element keeps the byte and reaches an assertion as part of the value. Every multi-line reader of the manifest stream therefore goes through `read_stream`: the same one strip per line, the same count, the same declaration on the same channel. Only the loop above keeps a copy of the strip, because it holds each line **unstripped** as an evidence operand, which an array of stripped values cannot carry. Nothing behind the invoke reads JSON with `jq`, since the crate parses with `serde_json`, so the adopter is untouched and only the harness handles the byte.

*The strip has one spelling and one site.* A `printf`-built `CR` variable and a quoted suffix pattern are taken **once** into a named scalar that both the count and the stored element read, so the two cannot disagree. The `.files` loop keeps its `$'\r'` spelling as the control.

*The owner is exercised against a **synthetic** CRLF stream in the preflight*, since no host a contributor runs emits the byte. It reds on the LF hosts too, prints nothing on the green path, and so buys no scenario in the parsed roster. **Its expectation is derived and never a literal.** A literal makes the arm assert what the **channel** delivered rather than what the **reader** did. So the arm reads the identical channel twice, once with a bare `mapfile -t` and once through the owner. It asserts the reader's own contract against that baseline: `mapfile -t` minus exactly one trailing carriage return per element, counted, and declared at that count. That is host-independent by construction.

Its vacuity guard is the strip having fired at all, since a channel delivering no carriage return anywhere covers nothing. A channel that does not carry the byte the synthetic stream was written with is a fact about the host, not a harness precondition: the uncovered case is declared with its bytes and the suite continues. A reader that mishandles a terminator is this harness's precondition and still refuses. That refusal prints the handed value, the returned value and one-strip-off-the-handed-value side by side. *A returned value equal to the handed one* is a strip that did not fire, and *a returned value equal to the baseline* is a channel that added a byte. No verdict that prints only a count tells those two apart.

**Once per failing profile**, and outside the per-path block because each is a fact about the run rather than about a path, the report also prints:

- the consumer's `git status --porcelain` and `git log -1 --stat`, truncated. They are the direct witness for the third row, since a worktree that has diverged from what `init` committed is the one shape that explains a disagreement set containing a binary;
- `core.autocrlf`, `core.eol` and `core.safecrlf` **with their origins** in both repositories, the mechanism behind the first row, where a value alone would not say which file set it;
- `git check-attr -a` for each sampled path in both repositories, the other half of that mechanism, since an attribute reaches a path the config does not.

Nothing is printed for completeness: every value has a reader in the table above or in the sentence that introduces it.

*The smoke-repository half of that attribute lookup never answers*, because the consumer is created under `INSTALLER_SMOKE_TMP_DIR`, outside the smoke's own repository. git refuses the lookup outright for a path outside the repository it is asked. The report prints that refusal labelled as a refusal rather than as an attribute report, and the refusal is itself the reading: the path's attribute chain is reachable from the consumer alone.

**The artifact digest is a filter-free control on the content question.** When the manifest records an `artifact` key, the report recomputes the artifact's SHA-256 from the tree and prints it beside the recorded `artifact.digest`. The hasher is the one its own preflight resolves, `sha256sum` or else `shasum -a 256`, in the bootstrap's order. SHA-256 over the file is taken by no git filter and in no repository context. Equal digests mean the artifact's bytes are exactly the bytes `init` published, so a `files`-row disagreement on that same path is not a content change. It cannot be an end-of-line conversion either, because git converts no blob it classifies binary. It is a **control**, so a matching digest speaks for the artifact alone and for no other path.

*The honest limit, stated rather than gated.* The report is failure-path code, and the only host that executes it is the host that fails, so no green run exercises it and no fixture pair can. What holds it is shape rather than coverage. It is a straight-line sequence of prints with no branch that can change the arm's verdict, and the `fail` that follows is the one that stood before it. A stale line can only make it less useful, never wrong-acting. It carries no knob for a related reason: a report enabled by a configuration no CI job sets is the dead-producer shape.

**The CI legs run the smoke once per declared platform, and each leg's posture is derived, never written.** `.github/workflows/gates.yml` carries one install-smoke leg per platform [docs/install.md §Requirements](https://github.com/checkwright/checkwright/blob/master/docs/install.md#requirements) declares, named as [§The install boundary](#the-install-boundary) names them. `native-artifacts-roster` reads the declaration's block and emits four outputs: `legs`, the producer's matrix; `index`, the same runner and held bit keyed by triple, because a job-level expression can index an object and cannot filter an array; `pwsh_legs`, the Windows triples; and `unix_legs`, the other triples less the battery's own, which `crate-tests-unix` tests ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §check-crate-arms](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#check-crate-arms)). A leg's `runs-on` and `continue-on-error` are read out of that index at its own triple. So a held triple's leg reports, a joined triple's leg binds, and flipping the declaration moves the posture with no workflow edit. A hard-coded `continue-on-error` would be the maintained copy that goes wrong once, silently, toward a joined platform whose red reds nothing. The triple a job-level expression spells is a read of the declaration: a triple that leaves it resolves no runner, and the workflow reds.

**The producer's matrix is the declaration, not the roster.** `native-artifacts` builds every declared platform, joined and held alike, through the release path's own build body ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload)), so a held platform is measured before it may join. A joined leg binds, since a red there is a published platform the release cannot produce. A held leg is a measurement, since a red there is why the platform stays held.

**Each leg installs the producer's upload, never a build of its own.** It downloads the artifacts by pattern rather than by name, because a name would spell a triple in a workflow step, a second spelling of the support commitment. Every leg takes the host triple from the bootstrap's detector through `host-target.sh`, which on Linux names the preferred glibc triple. It strips the artifact-name prefix to leave the `<dir>/<target>/` layout `INSTALLER_SMOKE_ARTIFACTS_DIR` takes, and places that target's artifact as the tree's own gate binary, since the smoke's pack step dispatches to it and builds none when handed artifacts. No leg compiles the crate or keeps a build cache: the producer compiled it on the same run, and the crate is most of a cold compile and changes on most pushes. While its triple is held, a leg's zero is the consumer half of [gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload)'s join pair and licenses no roster line alone; once the triple joins, a red is a support commitment broken. Each platform leg steers the smoke's roster at its host explicitly, so the caller-override branch has a live witness beside the baseline Linux leg's default.

**The baseline Linux leg is judged against the recorded baseline, and no other leg is.** Its smoke's status is captured, and `--diff-baseline installer_smoke` reds only where an arm deviates from `.workflow/validate-baseline.txt` ([evidence-kit/SPEC.md §Baseline manifest](../evidence-kit/SPEC.md#baseline-manifest)). The suite's per-arm parser makes each arm a scenario baselined `pass`, so an abort reds the arm that failed and every arm it skipped. The other legs bind on their own exit status, because the baseline's rows record how the arms behave on Linux and one scenario name cannot hold a second platform's population.

**The baseline Linux leg also runs both Linux artifacts on foreign hosts.** Inside an `alpine:3.22` and a `debian:12-slim` container, each pinned by digest, it asserts that the x86_64 musl artifact's `--list` exits 0 with a non-empty listing, and that the x86_64 glibc artifact's `--help` exits non-zero. The first witnesses that the static artifact serves a musl host and a glibc host below the glibc floor. The second witnesses the premise [§Selection](#selection)'s fallback rests on, that the glibc artifact does not run on either. The step names both triples through `host-target.sh`, the glibc one as the host's and the musl one as its fallback, so no triple is spelled in the workflow.

**Every leg checks out full history**, because the packer stamps the newest reachable tag ([§The packer](#the-packer)) and a shallow clone carries none, so a leg would silently exercise the fallback version. Each leg's `timeout-minutes` sits above its cold run with headroom and is widened before it is narrowed, since a timeout that reds on runner variance costs more than a long leg. `install-smoke-pwsh-windows` carries the widest, set from its measured run plus the margin the other legs carry, because its driver installs every profile on the slowest runners.

**Probe steps report and never fail**, and a red leg is read from its probe first. A macOS leg probes after the page's remedy block has run, so the probe reports the `PATH` an adopter following the page has. A leg whose label's architecture is its subject prints `uname -m`. On arm64 Windows, Git for Windows' POSIX layer runs emulated and reports x86_64, so the PowerShell leg asserts that the runner's own `rustc -vV` host triple is its matrix entry's before any step reads the host.

**A remedy step runs the page's block verbatim and adds nothing.** A macOS leg runs docs/install.md's `macos-remedy` block and a Windows leg its `windows-remedy` block, so a member the block lacks is the page's defect, fixed in the block. The macOS step then asserts that the adopter's next login shell resolves `bash` to Homebrew's prefix, and that the lines the block appended to `~/.zprofile` do so alone, after proving that a shell reading no profile does not.

**The native Windows leg** checks the tree out with LF line endings first ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload)), names a shell on every step ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §check-action-run-shell](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#check-action-run-shell)) and translates the scratch base once with `cygpath`. It prints the artifact name and never exports `GATE_SDK_NATIVE_BIN`, which would outrank the knob file `init` writes into each consumer.

*A native program takes a **relative** operand, and the filter builds the rest.* An argument that looks like an absolute POSIX path is rewritten into a host path on its way to a native Windows executable. `--arg b "/gates.list"` so reaches `jq.exe` as something under the interpreter's own install root, and `endswith` matches nothing. The harness concatenates a separator inside the filter and never passes one as the head of an argument. A diagnostic echoes such an operand back **through `jq`**, because a value printed by the shell is the value the shell holds, not the one the program was handed. A vacuity refusal prints the roster it searched as well as its verdict, so its zero is readable from the log.

**The payload every profile installs carries a real gate binary**, because the value claim is a claim about the product an adopter receives. The smoke compiles the crate for the host target, emits the digest sidecar beside it, and hands the pair to `--pack-installer --artifacts` before the loop starts. Each profile's battery is so the battery a covered platform actually gets. A main loop packing no artifact would make *every* profile an uncovered-platform install, and a value verdict measured there would be about the omitted battery wearing the shipped one's name. It costs no new program, since the preflight already requires `cargo` and `rustc`.

*A host-built artifact is a harness stand-in, and is labelled one where the rule it stands beside is cited.* [gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload) rules that the payload carries a prebuilt binary per declared target, *built by the release and never from a working tree*. The smoke builds from a working tree because it has no Release to draw on. That is a liberty this harness takes, not the payload rule relaxing. The publishing path still cannot build a *payload artifact*: what its `pack:` job builds is the tooling binary the arm runs as, never a binary the payload carries. The arm is still handed a directory it did not produce.

**The value claim is asserted over the loop, not inside it**, and it is two sentences: some profile catches the defect at all, and some profile *below* the payload-derived maximum catches it. The second is the load-bearing one. A defect only `full` catches is not value an adopter can choose, it is value they have to take everything for. Neither sentence names a gate, since naming one would be a second roster to maintain beside the recipe's own derivation, and the claim is about the battery rather than a member of it. Nor does either name a profile, for the reason the lattice assertions do not: which profiles catch a prose defect follows from the rosters. The arm turns into an assertion the claim the install page makes hardest to check: an install that is green, idempotent and reversible is still worth nothing until it catches something.

That is the **coverage** claim, and it speaks only for a covered platform. An adopter on an uncovered one gets a different claim, a **refusal**, because with every step of an install behind the invoke there is nothing left for an artifact-less host to proceed into. It has its own leg, since folding it into the coverage verdict would let a port pass per member while emptying a value class for every such install.

**The artifact-less refusal leg** drives a payload the packer itself produced with no artifact directory, which no other leg reaches. The artifact arm's refusals are driven against a payload the smoke mutated by hand, so without this leg nothing asserts that the *publishing path's* own artifact-free output refuses rather than proceeding. It asserts a refusal that **wrote nothing**, the tampered leg's shape, which tells a refusal apart from a warn-then-install. The refusal names the platform and carries the remedy line that tells this outcome from the broken-payload one. The leg then asserts the **same** refusal for `doctor`, for `diff` and for a bare invocation, because the refusal is the bootstrap's and precedes every verb. A leg asserting only `init` would pass on a bootstrap that had grown a per-verb branch, which the branchless argv rule forbids. It names a profile where the value claim names none, a scoping choice about which invocation to make rather than a derivation of which profiles catch what. The refusal is reached before the profile is ever read, and that is part of what the leg says.

**The license assertion** rides two places. The artifact-less leg's extraction must carry `package/LICENSE` and one `package/payload/<leaf>/LICENSE` per `package/payload/<leaf>/README.md`, each equal to the repository's root `LICENSE`, so [§The packer](#the-packer)'s placement is read off the publishing path's own output. The withholding arm then asserts, per profile, that each vendored kit root carries that same `LICENSE`, since the artifact-less package refuses before `init` writes anything.

**The profile lattice** is asserted against the installed payload, in four parts:

- every named kit resolves in the payload;
- the derived order has **exactly one minimum and exactly one maximum**, so the lattice is bounded;
- that maximum is the payload-derived profile;
- **gate rosters are monotone**: for every comparable pair, the smaller profile's gate set is contained in the larger's.

The fourth earns the recipe derivation's profile argument. What you experience is the battery, not the directory list, so "moving up only ever adds" is a claim about gates, and kit-set containment stops implying it the moment a roster varies by profile. Nothing here counts profiles; another is admitted exactly when it fits.

**The plan-parity arm** holds `init --dry-run` to [§init](#init)'s rule that the plan is the run's own code and not a second prediction of it. Before each profile's `init`, it runs `init --dry-run` on the fresh consumer. That run must leave the tree object and `git status` unchanged. The key set of the manifest it prints must equal the key set of the `checkwright.lock` the real run then writes. The comparison runs both ways, so a planned path the run never writes reds, and so does a recorded path the plan left out. An empty plan reds too, so parity never holds by vacuity.

A fresh consumer has no seed decision to make, since every seed is absent. A second leg therefore repeats the comparison at the payload-derived profile on a consumer already holding every surface `init` seeds. That set is read from what this loop's install at that profile recorded: every path outside a vendored kit and the gates directory. It is not listed in the smoke, so a kit that gains a seeded surface is planted with no edit here. A third leg re-seeds over that same set. An installed consumer's seeds are deleted and their recorded hashes made stale, as a seed body that changed across versions leaves them. The re-run must match its plan, record each re-seed at the hash of what it wrote, and report none as changed ([§What init seeds](#what-init-seeds)).

**The reversal arm** then runs on that same consumer, so every profile is installed *and* reversed. In order:

1. `diff` must exit 0 and report the freshly installed tree clean.
2. With one recorded `gate-sdk/` file's deletion committed, `update --dry-run` must exit 0, print its dry-run verdict and plan that file `(pending)`. The file stays absent and the tree object and worktree stay as they were. The deletion is then reset away.
3. `uninstall --dry-run` must name a non-zero removal count while leaving the tree object and `git status` exactly as they were.
4. After `uninstall`, the consumer's tree object must equal the one it had **before `init` ran**, the worktree must be clean, and no `checkwright.lock` may remain.

The two `--dry-run` steps are where the writes/does-not-write rule in [§The verbs](#the-verbs) is asserted for `update` and `uninstall`, and asserted behaviorally. A flag that parsed and then wrote anyway fails each, where a flag that merely existed would pass. The plan-parity arm holds `init` to the same rule.

**The tree-object equality is the load-bearing assertion, and it proves more than `uninstall`.** Nothing else here asserts that the manifest covers *everything* `init` wrote, since the per-profile check runs the other direction, every recorded entry against the tree. A file `init` wrote and failed to record survives the removal and breaks this equality. The arm so closes that hole as a side effect, for a *first* `init` here and for an upgrade hop's own write set in the cross-version reversal arm below. It is also the assertion form of the claim the install page makes: an install an evaluator can reverse.

The equality holds for a reason rather than by luck. The surfaces `init` seeds and then leaves alone (the queue file, the agent file, the evidence manifests, the workflow state) are recorded at `init`'s own hashes. This consumer never edits them, so the ordinary hash rule removes them. That same rule keeps them on a tree where an adopter *has* grown them, so the arm needs no special case either way.

**The download transport arm** verifies the packed tarball against a digest the smoke computes and extracts it with `tar` rather than npm. It runs the same `init`, the same post-conditions and the same reversal with `npm` and `node` **masked off `PATH`**, so `diff` and `uninstall` are proved Node-free at no extra pack cost. It runs against `full` alone rather than per profile. What the per-profile loop proves (the payload resolves and each profile's kit set is present) is profile-dependent. What this arm proves (the same payload reached the tree without Node) is transport-independent, and `full` is the largest payload with the widest `doctor` toolchain read. The smoke's preflight still requires `npm` and `node`, because packing needs them, and the masking is around this arm's `init` only.

Those transport arms carry two load-bearing properties, neither displacing the other. The offline tarball install turns "this is a one-shot vendoring installer, not a dependency channel" from a claim into an assertion: a package that installs and runs with no registry access after the fetch is not resolving anything on your behalf. The masked-`PATH` arm turns "the Release tarball needs no Node" from a sentence into an assertion. Without the masking the two arms would differ only in how the bytes arrived, and a latent Node dependency would pass silently on any machine that happens to have Node.

The mask is itself asserted rather than assumed: before the arm runs, each masked name must resolve to the shim, so a `PATH` that quietly failed to shadow the real interpreter reds instead of passing. Shims rather than deletion, because dropping every `PATH` entry carrying `node` would take `/usr/bin` with it wherever Node is installed there. The residue is that a payload merely *probing* for a Node binary still finds a name; one that *runs* it fails loudly and says which name it reached.

**The toolchain-free arm** points that same mask at `cargo` and `rustc`, and drives `doctor` and then a full `init` on a consumer that has neither. It asserts that `doctor` exits 0 and reports clean, and that it names neither masked tool in its report: a contributor-audience member is omitted from the adopter's verdict, not shown as informational ([§doctor](#doctor)). Through the same post-conditions every other arm runs, `init` must succeed and the vendored battery be green. `doctor` is asserted before `init` as well as inside it, because `init` reads only its exit status. The standalone verdict is what an adopter meets first and what every later refusal is downstream of.

That arm exists because nothing else here could see the defect it holds out. The smoke's own preflight *requires* `cargo` and `rustc`, legitimately, since it builds the binary the payload carries, so every other arm drives `doctor` and `init` on a machine that has them. **Masking is per-arm**, which lets this arm exist without weakening that preflight: the host requirement is unchanged and the build step still gets the real tools. The arm installs a *prebuilt* artifact with no toolchain on `PATH`, which is the claim the port directive rests on: an adopter takes the pre-compiled path, and nothing on it compiles. The mechanism is the existing Node-free mask rather than a knob, because a knob that suppressed a roster member would be a second, test-only audience axis no adopter exercises. A masked `PATH` is what a machine with no Rust toolchain actually is.

**The `jq`-less arm** asserts what a machine without `jq` is told, and its claim is that the verbs **do not need `jq` at all**. Nothing behind the invoke reads JSON with it, so the arm's oracle is a verb that runs clean where a verb shelling out to `jq` fails. On this `PATH` the two are distinguishable and nowhere else are they. The claim reaches past the verbs to what they install ([§Requirements](#requirements)). In this order:

- **`doctor` in a directory with no install** exits 0 and names `jq` nowhere.
- **`init --profile` at the lattice minimum** exits 0 on the `jq`-less `PATH`, and `doctor` inside that install exits 0 and names `jq` nowhere.
- **`init` at a profile whose kit set carries guard-kit**, found through the harness's own profile reader and run in a fresh consumer, exits 0, and `doctor` inside it names `jq` nowhere. The arm names guard-kit because it drives that kit's hook, not to restate an audience field.
- **The installed guard answers a payload**: fed a read-only command, the wired member, `--hook shell-guard` on the gate binary, exits 0 with an allow envelope on the `jq`-less `PATH`. An allow is a payload read and a render, and it is neither the front end's absent-binary decline nor an empty stdout.
- **`diff` and `uninstall --dry-run`** run no `doctor` precondition, so they read the minimum's manifest and reach their answer. Each must **exit 0** and say nothing about `jq`, the arm's positive evidence that the read itself is `jq`-free.

The smoke's preflight requires `jq`, and this harness reads every manifest assertion above with it. **Masking is per-arm** here for a reason the other two masks do not have: a mask on the harness's own `PATH` would disarm the assertions rather than the installer. The mask rides the verb's `PATH` alone, and the preflight is unchanged.

**This mask is by absence, a different instrument from the other two.** The Node-free and toolchain-free arms ask whether the payload ever *reaches* a program, so a shim that fails loudly and names itself is the right tool. This arm asks what a machine *without* `jq` is told, and a shim is a `jq` that is present: `command -v jq` resolves it, and the verbs never meet an absent program. So the arm builds a directory of links to every program on `PATH` except `jq` and runs the verbs against that. The farm is one helper shared with the `bash`-less arm below:

- **It is derived from the live `PATH`**, never from a maintained list of the programs these verbs happen to use, so it cannot fall out of date.
- **The exclusion is the masked program's case-folded stem.** That covers `jq.exe`, which shell suffix resolution would hand back, and the `.cmd` the crate's `PATHEXT` search would find, without naming any suffix.
- **A directory is farmed only when it carries the masked program**, and every other directory stays on the arm's `PATH` verbatim, which takes nothing from the mask.
- **The mask is proved in both directions.** The masked program must resolve to nothing, and a control program must still resolve and **run**. `command -v` is a stat satisfied by an entry that will not execute, so a farm of unusable entries would fail every verb for a reason unrelated to the mask.

**The `bash`-less arm** proves that a profile whose kit set owes no `bash` installs and commits on a machine without one. It builds its `PATH` by the same absence farm, `bash` masked, and proves the mask both ways. `/bin/sh` is not masked: it is the shell git runs hooks with ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §gen-pre-commit](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#gen-pre-commit)). The arm runs the unix bootstrap as the page does, through `sh` resolved on the farm, so nothing from the bootstrap to the hooks can find `bash` on `PATH`. Before the first verb it proves the farm's `sh` runs, as it proves the farm's `git` does, since a farm that dropped `sh` would fail every step for a reason that is not `bash`. In order:

- **`doctor` with no install** exits 0 and renders `bash` as `not probed`, naming the audience it is owed by. That line is asserted and **no roster is taken out of it**. Which of [§doctor](#doctor)'s two renderings it carries, the resolved kit list or the predicate, depends on whether the derivation reached a kit root. A harness parsing names out of it would read the predicate as a roster no kit matches the moment the audience becomes derived, classifying every profile as owing nothing.
- **The arm's subjects are the profiles whose own installed `doctor` report carried no probed `bash` row**, recorded by the profile loop above. That is [§doctor](#doctor)'s verdict rule read directly: an owed member is probed, rendered and sets the verdict; a not-owed one is not rendered; an undecided one is rendered unprobed and cannot set it. A selection whose derived audience reaches no kit root still produces the undecided rendering, and the lattice minimum is exactly that case. A probed row is so the only rendering that means owed. Each selection's own verdict is the answer, read off `doctor` rather than named here, and the lattice minimum must be among the subjects.
- **At each such profile**, in a fresh consumer, `init --profile` exits 0 and each command the follow-up block printed is executed and exits 0. `--install-hooks` is among them, wiring the hooks the next two steps commit through. One clean commit then lands with the pre-commit hook's summary line printed. One commit planting a home-directory path is refused, the refusing gate read off the hook's own `pre-commit: <gate> failed` line and held to the consumer's registry.
- The suite is unix-hosted and refuses a native Windows host; the PowerShell legs carry Windows (below).

A `bash` lookup anywhere on that path fails the step that made it, and that step's message names the command.

**The PowerShell driver carries native Windows.** `installer/consumer-smoke/run-smoke.ps1`, run under `pwsh` by each `install-smoke-pwsh-windows` matrix entry after its other steps, takes the same per-file `no-port` disposition as `run-smoke.sh`, on [§The port disposition](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#the-port-disposition)'s ground, declared in its header. It prints one header line per arm, and its reach is five coverage classes: init, battery, hooks, upgrade and uninstall. For each profile in `profiles.list` plus `full`, in a fresh consumer:

- it runs `init --profile` through `bin/checkwright.ps1` from the packed tarball, whose payload carries the producer's upload for the host, and asserts the manifest records the profile and that artifact;
- it reads the profile's own `doctor` report, and a profile owing no `bash` there has every `bash` stripped from `PATH` for the steps below, the system directory's WSL launcher excepted, while the rest keep it;
- it runs the battery through the binary `init` placed with `--run`, green and leaving the worktree clean;
- it runs the printed `--install-hooks` line, then commits once clean, reading `pre-commit: <N> gate(s) passed.`, and once refused on a planted home-directory path, reading `pre-commit: <gate> failed (see above).` with the gate held to the consumer's registry;
- it resets to the install commit and runs `uninstall`, and the tree object must equal the pre-init one.

Once, at the lattice minimum, the upgrade arm runs `update` from the tree packed at the next patch version, a tarball the leg's pack step builds beside the first, and asserts the lock's version moved, the profile was re-read and the battery is green. The arms `run-smoke.sh` runs and this driver does not stay on the four unix legs: seed, demo, companion, plan parity, artifact-less refusal, download, toolchain-free, jq-less, cross-version and newer-verb reversal, hooked move, seam, narrowing, artifact, withholding, follow-up, doctor, value.

**The upgrade arm** drives a cross-version run, because every arm above installs at one version and re-runs at that same one. It packs a second tarball a patch version higher, installs `starter` from the first, and has the adopter edit and commit two vendored files. It then runs the second package's `init` with no flags at all. Only that reaches three behaviours:

- the manifest's version comparison falling *through* in the upgrade direction rather than refusing;
- the profile re-read from the manifest when none is passed;
- the ownership claim re-applying the payload around a file that has changed since `init` wrote it: left alone, reported, and still the adopter's afterwards.

The roster is asserted directly rather than only through that effect, because two different manifests leave the same intact file on this hop and neither survives the next. An entry dropped altogether reads as *never installed* on the following run, and an entry recorded at the adopter's own hash reads as *unchanged*. Both would let the next `init` claim the path, so both are named apart. Before its first pack, and on either pack's failure branch, the arm prints the free space and the scratch tree's size through a witness that never changes a verdict. A pack that dies printing nothing is still readable from a finished log: if the scratch filesystem ran out, the witness shows it.

The second edited file is the **relinquish subject**, and it is what makes the arm reach [§The manifest](#the-manifest)'s exit rule at all. The pack step assembles every version from one worktree, so two hops would otherwise carry byte-identical payloads and no path would ever leave a kit's shipped set. The arm therefore deletes that path from the *extracted package's own* `payload/` before the hop runs, rather than through a flag on the publishing path, which leaves the publisher no way to ship a payload with a hole in it. The subject is chosen against a criterion rather than by taste: a `starter`-kit payload file `init` records in `files` that no `init` step and neither generated projection reads. Dropping it exercises the roster's exit condition and nothing else. On this hop the file must be untouched on disk and must **still be on the roster at the hash `init` wrote there**. Disowning it here is exactly what would arm the next release to write through the adopter's edits.

It then chains a **third** version onto the same consumer with no fresh edit, because one hop only shows the protection starting. The second hop is where it either persists or inverts. The already-edited, already-reported file must still be the adopter's and must still be reported, and the manifest the first hop wrote must still carry it. This hop's payload also **re-adds** the relinquished path, which is where the ownership rule pays. That path must meet the carried claim, be refused, be reported, and keep `init`'s own hash on the roster. Without the exit rule this hop overwrites it silently, so the defect is reproduced end to end rather than argued about. Each version is derived from the one packed before it, and the arm refuses to run unless the derivation is strictly higher, so neither hop can quietly turn into a second test of the downgrade refusal.

**The first hop's clean-worktree assertion carries a tripwire**, because the assertion is evidence only over a hop that rewrote something. A hop that rewrites nothing beyond the manifest passes it for a reason unrelated to correctness. Before asserting the worktree clean, the hop therefore asserts a **non-zero** count of *live* registry members and a **placed artifact** in the consumer's own manifest. It reads the registry rather than the run's output, because the registry is what a later run and a reviewer both read. Its failure names the remedy: **repair the hop, never drop the assertion.** Its scope is the first hop; the second hop's clean-worktree assertion carries no tripwire, and widening it is a separate judgment.

**Every cross-version pack carries the artifact directory the main pack used.** An artifact-free payload does not install at all, so a hop that packed without one would assert a refusal where the arm needs a completion. The bytes are the ones the build step already staged, so the hops differ in version and in the relinquish this arm performs, and in nothing else.

**The cross-version reversal arm** reverses a consumer that crossed all three of those versions. Every other reversal in the suite reverses a *first* `init`, and the upgrade arm asserts no reversal at all. It is its own scratch consumer at the lattice minimum with **no adopter edit**. It re-runs the upgrade arm's two already-extracted packages with no flags, so it costs no pack, and the edited case belongs to the protection branch below, since an adopter edit is what tree-object equality cannot host. It then drives the reversal arm's `diff`, `uninstall --dry-run` and `uninstall` with the **latest** package's verb, what an adopter holds after an upgrade, against a roster three versions old. The tree object must come back to the one the consumer had before its first `init`.

*What that reaches is narrower than a recorded hash moving, and the limit is the harness's rather than the assertion's.* The arm assembles every version from one worktree, so no vendored path's content differs between hops. It does not exercise a hash that changed under a path that stayed. The shape changes it does cross are path additions and removals. What it exercises, and nothing else here does, is twofold. A tree whose payload lost a path on one hop and regained it on the next must still be **wholly removable**. The roster must cover an **upgrade** hop's write set: a rewritten manifest, regenerated projections, whatever a future release adds. The arm proves its own premise before it reverses, in the tripwire idiom above. The relinquish must still be in effect, the manifest must record the third version, and the relinquished path must still be on the roster. Each failure names the re-scope, never a licence to drop the assertion.

**The newer-verb reversal arm** reverses an install with a later release's verb and no upgrade between, the case the one-line install meets, since it fetches its own release whatever the manifest records ([§uninstall](#uninstall)). A fresh consumer with no adopter edit takes the lattice minimum at the first version, and its manifest is asserted to record that version. The upgrade arm's first extracted package then runs `uninstall`, and its payload lacks the relinquished path, so only the roster can name that file. The tree object must come back to the one before `init`, with the worktree clean and no manifest left. It runs `uninstall` alone: a later release's `diff` and `update --dry-run` over an older install answer an upgrade question, which is the upgrade arm's.

**The hooked move arm** commits an install's own moves through the hooks it vendors, which no arm above does: each installs, re-runs and upgrades with no hook installed. A fresh consumer takes the lattice minimum, runs `--install-hooks` through the binary the seam names, and asserts an executable pre-commit hook. It then re-runs `init` at the **maximum** profile, and the move must land as one commit with the worktree clean, and the new registry must carry `check-gate-tamper`, so the move meets the gate that judges a gate file co-staged with the manifest.

Next it upgrades from a **copy** of the upgrade arm's first package whose payload gate library carries one appended comment line. Every pack is assembled from one worktree, so an unmutated hop stages no gate file and the gate's isolation assertion never opens. The copy leaves the package other arms read untouched. The hop must commit, move the manifest's version and leave the worktree clean, and its commit must carry both the gate library and the manifest, or the hop never staged the shape under test. A **control** closes the arm: a gate-library edit co-staged with a product file must be refused, with `pre-commit: check-gate-tamper failed` among the hook's lines, so the two commits are green on the manifest's standing rather than on a disarmed gate.

**The seam arm** covers the two surfaces `init` rewrites on every run, a `templates/*-config.sh` destination and gate-sdk's `msg-patterns.list`, which no arm above reaches. The upgrade arm's subject is an ordinary vendored file on the plain claim-and-copy path, so those arms exercise a different file class and stay true without covering this one. This arm re-runs at the **same version with no flags**. The class needs no upgrade and no `--force`, so an arm that only ran across versions would attribute it to a path it does not live on. It is its own scratch consumer at the **maximum** profile, the only profile whose kit set is fixed by the payload rather than by a roster judgment, so both surfaces it edits are present by construction. It is its own consumer because an adopter edit inside the per-profile loop would break the file-by-file agreement that loop exists to assert. After the adopter edits and commits both, the re-run must leave both byte-identical, name both as changed, and still record `init`'s hash for each rather than the adopter's. It reuses the already-installed package, so it costs no second pack.

*Its byte-identity comparison is read through the terminator owner rather than with `cmp`.* A `cmp` between `jq`'s stdout and a crate-written file is a comparison of channels, and fails wherever they differ however canonical the writer is. Line-wise after the one declared strip keeps every axis the assertion is about: the key order at every nesting level, which is what `-S` tests, the indentation, the line count, and any trailing byte that is not exactly one carriage return. It gives up only the axis the channel owns.

**The protection branch chains onto that consumer** rather than onto the reversal arm, because an adopter edit is exactly what breaks tree-object equality. This arm already has two edited, committed vendored files, the case that reaches `uninstall`'s keep branch. After its own assertions it appends a byte to the installed gate binary, at the path the seam names, and commits it, so the one mismatched row that is never the adopter's rides the same run. It then runs `diff`, which must exit **1** and name both files. Then `uninstall` must keep both, report both, and remove every other recorded file, the tampered binary included and never reported as kept. It must leave a `checkwright.lock` carrying `schema` and a `files` map of exactly those two paths **at `init`'s hashes, not the adopter's**. That is the upgrade arm's apart-naming, for the same reason: an entry dropped reads as never-installed, an entry at the adopter's hash reads as unchanged, and either would let the next `init` write through them.

That residual object is asserted for **shape**, not only for field presence, because the single-writer contract in [§The manifest](#the-manifest) is what an accessor cannot check: a missing key and a present-but-null key both read back as the empty string. The assertions therefore run on the captured manifest text itself. `has("artifact")` must be false, so the omitted flag left the key absent rather than null. Re-piping the object through a recursive sort must reproduce it byte for byte, so the sort reached every nesting level rather than the top one. Both run here because this is the one call site that emits the no-identity, no-artifact shape; the per-profile loop's fresh install exercises the other writer field by field.

**The narrowing arm** is the only arm that moves a consumer *down* the lattice: it installs the maximum profile and re-runs `init` at the minimum. Every other re-run holds the profile fixed, so none reaches the state where `files` outlives `kits`. That state is the ordinary consequence of the carry-forward rule, which keeps every once-vendored path on the roster while the recorded kit set shrinks. For every seam path the narrowed manifest records, it asserts that the path still resolves to the consumer's **own** file. A `kits`-stripped copy of that same manifest, the residual shape, must resolve it the same way. Then `doctor` must name the consumer's own `gates.list` as the registry it inspected. It asserts its own premise too: at least one seam path checked, and at least one of those genuinely shadowed by a vendored fixture tree. Otherwise the resolver has nothing to be ambiguous about, and a green result would mean only that the payload changed shape.

*Its honest limit.* Only the recorded paths are asserted on, and the config seam is written on the artifact placement path alone, so on a payload carrying no prebuilt binary the arm would resolve the registry and not the seam. It runs against the main payload, which carries one, so both are checked. The arm still refuses to *demand* the seam, because that would fail it on the payload rather than on the resolver. The residual shape keeps it biting either way: with no `kits` key, a tail match returns a vendored fixture for `gates.list` too.

**The selection arm** runs one consumer at the lattice minimum ([§Selecting kits and gates](#selecting-kits-and-gates)), naming no gate or kit literally: it reads each name off the package, from the payload's kit roots, the minimum's installed registry and each gate's `# install:` line. `init` passes `--with-kit` naming a payload kit outside the minimum's set, `--without-gate` naming the first member of the minimum's registry, and `--with-gate` naming an `on-surface` member of the added kit. The arm asserts one commit, `kits` holding both sets, the registry lacking the dropped member and carrying the added one, the manifest's `selection` equal to what was passed, and the battery's resolved kit roots equal to `kits`. It does not assert the battery green, since an `on-surface` member may red on a tree lacking its surface. A bare re-run must leave the tree object unchanged. A re-run with `--no-selection` must restore the minimum's registry and `kits`, record no `selection`, and leave the added kit's directory on disk. Then `--without-kit` naming a minimum kit, an unknown kit and an unresolvable `--with-gate` must each exit 2 and write nothing.

**Every arm above rides [§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary)'s placement outcome**, because the payload they install carries this run's artifact. The binary is written, an `artifact` key reaches the manifest, nothing is omitted, and each profile's battery dispatches its `.gate` members through the placed path. That outcome is the `--install place-artifact` op's, so the same arms assert that op. An artifact-less payload is told apart from a covered one before any verb runs, by the refusal leg above.

**The binary is built rather than fabricated**, which is what makes the placement branch worth exercising at all. A stand-in with a matching digest would drive the same code while leaving the one thing most likely to break covered by nothing: the real build's digest agreeing with what `init` verifies before writing. The smoke therefore asserts:

- the target `init` selected, against the triple the bootstrap's detector gives through the helper, and that triple's architecture against `rustc`'s wherever `rustc` is present, the one derivation independent of the detector;
- the recorded digest, against the one the build step emitted;
- the binary executable at the path the config seam names;
- both that path and the seam on the manifest roster.

**The artifact arm covers the outcomes a single install cannot show.** It takes its own extraction of that same tarball and mutates the copy, rather than packing a second time:

- a host **off** the roster refuses, naming the platform and offering no adopter action;
- a **tampered** artifact refuses with the consumer's tree object unchanged and no manifest written;
- a **declared** target whose artifact is gone refuses as a publisher defect the adopter can act on.

All three are bootstrap outcomes, decided before the invoke, so the arm is unmoved by the placement step going behind it. The arm asserts each refusal's own **message and remedy**, and then asserts that the two refusals an adopter meets **differ**. The exit status does not tell them apart, and an arm that read it alone would see one answer where an adopter must be given two: one they can do nothing about, and one they fix by re-downloading. That comparison keeps [§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary)'s four outcomes from collapsing into each other.

**Three fallback cases follow wherever the hand-off carries a foreign-architecture preferred artifact**, as every CI Linux leg's does. That artifact verifies and cannot start here, so it stands in for a preferred artifact that does not run. Each payload is placed from producer uploads with their sidecars:

- **falls back**: the foreign artifact as the host's preferred one, beside the host's fallback upload. `init` completes and records the fallback triple.
- **held preferred**: the fallback alone rostered. `init` completes on it.
- **no fallback**: the foreign artifact alone rostered. `init` meets the does-not-run refusal, asserted distinct from the other two refusals.

A host with no such hand-off, every local run included, skips the three and says so. Mutating an extracted package rather than adding a flag to the publishing path leaves the publisher no way to ship a payload with a hole in it.

**The arm also drives step 4's `shasum` fallback**, which no runner reaches on its own, since every CI image ships a `sha256sum`. It masks `sha256sum` by absence with the same farm the `bash`-less arm uses and proves the mask both ways. `sha256sum` resolves to nothing, and the farm's `shasum -a 256 -c` accepts the payload's sidecar. That control is a check and never a computation, so the smoke adds no second producer of the digest ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §check-gate-substrate-parity](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#check-gate-substrate-parity)). Under that `PATH` an `init` through the bootstrap installs, and the tampered artifact is refused by the digest comparison with nothing written, so the branch is shown both to verify and to compare. A host with no `shasum` says so and skips.

The arm gains nothing from this: the **smoke** builds and hands it a directory, while the publishing path never builds a payload artifact, so a locally built binary can never substitute for a released one.

**The smoke steers its own roster.** A single host build satisfies `--artifacts` only while the roster declares this host alone. Pack refuses a roster target no leg built, and refusing is right, because a payload missing a declared target is broken rather than narrower. The smoke therefore narrows its roster through `GATE_SDK_NATIVE_TARGETS_FILE` ([gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Layout and configuration](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#layout-and-configuration)). **A build for a target this host cannot run is refused**, on the ground `native/targets.list` gives: it would publish an artifact no run has executed. A host's native build is not that: the host runs it, and the smoke executes it.

*That guard is unconditional where its stated ground is not.* It refuses a roster wider than this host *before* reaching the artifact hand-off branch and without consulting it. A run pointed at a complete producer hand-off, which could satisfy `--artifacts` for every declared target, so refuses byte-identically to one holding nothing, naming a host-build remedy that does not describe the hand-off path. The guard is stricter than the reason it gives. It blocks nothing, since every caller either steers at its own host or lets the smoke self-steer.

The smoke derives a one-line roster from this host's triple and points that knob at it **unless the caller has already set it**. Three consequences follow:

- A caller that steers explicitly keeps its own roster, so the override branch stays a live path rather than a fixture-only one.
- A local `bash installer/consumer-smoke/run-smoke.sh` survives a multi-line shipped roster instead of blocking on it.
- The unsteered Linux leg carries no assertion that the shipped roster is packable. The `native-artifacts` producer building every declared platform on every run asserts the shipped roster's producibility directly.

**The narrowing removes one reader's subject, and that reader gets a planted witness rather than an argument.** Pack's refusal of a *declared target no leg built* is the one verdict here that reds on finding a target instead of on finding none. A roster narrowed to the host makes it unreachable on every ordinary path, where every other affected reader is monotone under the narrowing and clears by inspection. The pack arm therefore plants that case, packing against a roster carrying a second target the artifact directory has nothing for, and asserts both the refusal and its cause. Its log line is `pack: a declared target with no artifact directory refused, not packed narrower`. Read it as distinct from the artifact arm's `declared target with no artifact: refused, not omitted`, which is `init` refusing a broken *payload* after the pack succeeded: one shape of mistake, two verbs, two witnesses.

**A platform leg's steered roster makes the artifact branch live on that host.** A per-platform install-smoke leg steers `GATE_SDK_NATIVE_TARGETS_FILE` at a single-host roster, and the packer copies that roster into the payload verbatim. `target_of_host()` maps the leg's host to a triple, so the roster comparison matches and `select_artifact` takes its artifact-present branch on a platform `native/targets.list` does not declare. A claim that code below that branch is dormant *because the shipped roster carries no such line* is therefore false on every platform leg. A site costed dormant on that ground is a live site.

**It takes three knobs.** `INSTALLER_SMOKE_TMP_DIR` is the scratch base, and the smoke writes nothing inside the worktree. The crate's build output lands in gitignored build space, and the artifact directory it assembles lives under that scratch, so the clean-worktree precondition keeps its meaning. It needs that clean worktree, because the pack step refuses to stamp a commit the payload does not match.

`INSTALLER_SMOKE_ARTIFACTS_DIR` is the **artifact hand-off**, the difference between a run that exercises a release-shaped artifact and one that exercises a harness stand-in. Set it to a `<dir>/<target>/` tree a producer already filled and the smoke installs *those* bytes. It builds nothing and recomputes nothing: the sidecar that arrives is the sidecar the producer emitted beside the bytes, so [gate-sdk/SPEC.md §Consumer payload](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#consumer-payload)'s one-producer rule reaches across the hop unbroken. Its live setters are exactly the install-smoke legs in `.github/workflows/gates.yml` that consume the producer's upload, each a deployed configuration rather than a test-only one. Outside them it is unset. **Read the setter set by that predicate and never as a roster**: a platform joining or leaving the declaration moves the set, and consuming the hand-off is what its members have in common.

`INSTALLER_SMOKE_TARBALL_OUT` is the **tarball hand-out**: set it to an existing directory and the smoke copies the tarball it packed there, with a digest sidecar it emits beside it, before its scratch is torn down. Its live setter is the baseline Linux leg, whose next step runs the install page's `unix-install` block against those bytes ([§Requirements](#requirements), the install blocks). The hand-out lets that step move the tarball and its sidecar rather than build, hash and pack a second payload beside the smoke's. That leg downloads the producer's upload and uploads nothing, so [gate-sdk/SPEC.md §check-gate-substrate-parity](../gate-sdk/SPEC.md#check-gate-substrate-parity)'s one-producer rule lets it compute no digest of its own.

`cargo` and `rustc` join the preflight alongside the tools every other arm needs, and refuse there when either is missing: a machine that cannot compile the crate has not falsified the install path. That refusal relaxes **on the hand-off path alone**. A host handed a prebuilt artifact was never asked to compile anything, so refusing it for a missing compiler would refuse the exact case the knob exists to serve. The host triple is the bootstrap detector's answer on every host, read through `installer/consumer-smoke/host-target.sh`, which extracts `target_of_host` and the two functions it calls from `installer/bin/checkwright.sh` on the shape [§The gate binary](#the-gate-binary) pins and holds no mapping of its own, so the smoke and the bootstrap cannot disagree about which artifact a host takes. On a Linux host that triple is the glibc one `rustc` builds natively. Where the detector's triple is not `rustc`'s host, the build passes `--target` that triple and a failed build names the `rustup target add` remedy. With `--fallback <triple>` the helper prints the triple the bootstrap's `fallback_of_target` names instead, extracted the same way, which is how the artifact arm's fallback cases and the baseline leg's foreign-host step name the static triple without spelling it.

**What it costs to run.** On one Linux developer machine the whole smoke takes about 272 seconds: four profiles × install + battery + value arm, the binary-less leg, four packs, an npm install and one release build of the crate. It so fits one ordinary foreground invocation and needs no session-window planning, and the clean worktree it holds is held for minutes rather than for a working session. Re-measure rather than trust the figure if a decision turns on it.

*Why the payload has no gate of its own.* The obvious sibling check would assert that the packed payload matches the repository's kit roots. It is deliberately not a gate. The payload exists only at pack time, so the gate would have to run `npm pack` at commit time, putting a network-capable toolchain in the pre-commit path and breaking the hermeticity every other gate keeps. The property is covered here instead, in the tier that can afford it. The pack step derives the payload from the same kit-root set the battery itself resolves, and the smoke runs `doctor` from the payload for *every* profile.
